Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Those tiny black flies are only part of the story. A raw potato slice on the soil can reveal what's underneath for next to nothing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You water your houseplant, and a little cloud of tiny black flies lifts off the soil. A minute later, they're on the window. Fungus gnats turn up in many homes once fall arrives, and they can hang around all winter. The next batch is already growing in the pot, and a fungus gnat potato trap is an easy way to find them.

Before you read up on how to get rid of fungus gnats, take a look at what's going on in the pot. The adult flies you keep swatting don't feed on your plants, but their larvae are a different story. Those live in the damp potting mix just under the surface, out of sight unless you go digging.

One raw potato saves you the digging. Lay a slice on the soil, and the larvae come up to feed on it. Lift it a couple of days later, and whatever is in the pot is often feeding on the underside. Odds are there's a potato in the pantry already, so finding out costs you pretty much nothing, really.

A fungus gnat's whole life happens in or around the pot. They're small flies, often in the genus Bradysia, and a female can lay up to 200 eggs in damp potting mix. Once they hatch, the larvae eat for a couple of weeks and pupate near the surface, and new adults show up a week or so later. At room temperature, that's roughly three to four weeks per generation – so a few flies in October can be a lot more by the holidays.

It's the larvae doing the eating. Their usual food is fungi and rotting organic matter, but they'll go after fine root hairs too. While a minor infestation won't usually do any harm, enough of them can damage roots and stunt growth, especially in seedlings and young plants. Watch for something like a tiny worm: clear or whitish, no legs, a shiny black head, ¼ inch (6 mm) long at most.

Cut a raw potato into slices about ¼ inch (6.4 mm) thick. Set one cut side down on the potting mix, and press it lightly so it sits flat. That contact is the whole trick. Larvae move up to the potato as a food source and gather on the moist underside where it touches the soil.

Give it a day or two before the first look. Flip the slice and check its underside, then the soil where it sat, for tiny clear larvae. Against dark, wet potting mix, they're hard to pick out, though, so a magnifying glass, like this Rongon 10X folding pocket magnifier from Amazon, helps a lot. Nothing there yet? Set it back down for another day or two. Sometimes larvae can take a few days to find the potato.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Don't leave it there for good, though. Raw potato breaks down in damp soil, and a rotting slice is just more of the decaying material larvae feed on. Toss the old one in the trash, larvae and all, and put down a fresh slice. Used like this, potato slices for fungus gnats let you track whether the numbers are dropping. Eggs won't show up on it. They don't feed, so they stay put in the mix.

So, do potatoes kill fungus gnats? Not really. The potato doesn't poison anything – it just draws feeding larvae up from the roots, and tossing a slice with larvae on it removes those ones. Eggs, pupae, and the adults flying around the room aren't affected.

Use the potato to check on things, then reach for something else to fix it. Say the slice comes up clean. That's nice, but it doesn't mean the pot's clear. Maybe there are only a few larvae, or they weren't feeding much. If flies keep hanging around, put down another slice.

Too much water keeps a lot of fungus gnat problems going. Short days and cool rooms slow houseplants down in fall and winter, so they use less water. Water like it's still July, and the mix stays wet, which eggs and larvae love. Let the top inch (2.5cm) dry before watering again. Empty the saucer, and make sure the pot drains. Old mix holds extra water as it breaks down. If a plant's due for repotting, look for a fresh mix with perlite for drainage, like the Back to the Roots Indoor Potting Mix, available from Walmart.

Yellow sticky traps are for the adults. Push a few into the pot – you can buy sticky traps cheaply from Amazon. Each female stuck to one won't lay any more eggs, and the count tells you if things are improving. Down in the soil, the larvae aren't touched. If the gnats won't let up, try Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis subsp. israelensis), a naturally occurring soil bacterium. Despite the name, it isn't the Bt sprayed on caterpillars. This strain targets only fly larvae.

Summit Mosquito Bits use Bti to control both mosquito and fungus gnat larvae. Rather than scattering the granules on the soil, it's best to soak them in water for about 30 minutes, then apply that water to your houseplant soil. Repeat application about every five days, since Bti doesn't last long indoors.

Beneficial nematodes (Steinernema feltiae), such as BioLogic's Scanmask nematodes, are another organic option. These microscopic roundworms seek out fungus gnat larvae in potting soil. They enter the larvae and release bacteria that kill them, then feed and reproduce inside their bodies. It's pretty gruesome, but effective. They arrive alive in the mail, so use them right away. Keep the soil moist and the temperature between 60 and 90°Fahrenheit (16–32°C), or they won't work. Whichever you buy, check that the label allows indoor potted plants, then follow it.

Catching larvae early makes a fungus gnat problem much easier to control. A few larvae in one pot make for a far smaller job than a houseful of flies a month from now – and a potato slice is a cheap way to see whether your houseplant soil is hiding them.

So keep a potato around this winter. Set a fresh slice down whenever the flies show up again, and go easier on the watering while days are short. Fungus gnats have a much harder time of it once the top of the soil dries out between drinks!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7984. The Cool Dad’s Guide to Father’s Day

Happy Father’s Day, from one cool dad to the next.

If you follow Fatherly’s Instagram handle, you may notice that we’ve been talking to a number of cool dads lately. We start by asking them about some of the little things that bring us the most joy, like the best movie to watch with your kid (among the answers, The Princess Bride, Zootopia, Sketch, Hook), the clothing they’re passionate about (black t-shirts, black button downs, and Jordan 1s are popular) and the music we blast for our kids (from Michal Jackson to Nirvana, Chance the Rapper to The Lone Bellow)

But look past these small insights and you’ll find successful men who are eager to talk about their kids. The variety of responses show how every dad has their own take, their unique philosophy about being a good man, a strong partner, and a great parent. It also shows how much solidarity there is in being a dad.

Max Holloway, the dominant UFC fighter says he believes in being strict, but “it’s not just me being hard on him and busting his chops, but also encouraging him and telling him he did a good job.”

Tony Hale, who needs no introduction if you’re a fan of Toy Story, Arrested Development, or Veep, admits he was more of a helicopter parent, one whose kids—now in college—know that, "Hey, when you need me, I'm always going to be here.”

Colton Underwood, the former reality star and pro football player is serious about the job: “I have the responsibility that he grows up to be a great human being that does good in the world.” While Maurice Edu, who you’ve no doubt been hearing calling the World Cup shots on Fox Sports, finds fatherhood to be fairly effortless because “I always knew I wanted to be a father, but until I actually became one, I didn't realize how much I wanted it."

Minneapolis lawyer and former mayoral candidate Jazz Hampton believes that “Fatherhood is how you show up for your own kids and the rest of the world as well, and how you teach your kids to show up for other people.” Meanwhile, the “Tired Dad” Jon Gustin notes that parenting is tough, but rewarding — a “badge of honor that we wear because we're showing up in all areas.”

Then there’s Tom Llamas, our latest Cool Dad and the anchor of "NBC Nightly News” and "Top Story with Tom Llamas" on NBC News NOW. In a recent chat, Llamas reminded me that we, dads who are parenting now in 2026, weren’t the first and won’t be the last. Our parents struggled and cared and went through it all with their kids, and so did their dads, and theirs before them.

Llamas’ father, a Cuban refugee and dentist, was a big role model to him. “I learned a lot of great lessons from my dad,” Llamas says, “and then also try to be a better dad, and I think that's what my dad tried to do, too. He had a good dad, but he tried to be a better dad, and I'm trying to do the same thing.”

Tom Llamas’ parents fled Cuba for Florida during Fidel Castro’s takeover of the country. Years later, in 1979, Tom was born. Llamas remembers a childhood in Miami that was a stark contrast to life in Cuba, under the rule of a dictator in a harsh economic economic environment. Primarily, he remembers his parents being there for him. “They would close the office early, like when I had sports, you know, to go and see me. Or if I had a school event they would close the office early, and for a small business that's income that you're not bringing in.”

He continues, “I'm grateful to have parents that always supported me in whatever I wanted to do — whether it was playing sports as a little boy, or when I got into journalism, or when I was into speech and debate in high school, to helping me when I had internships, because back when I was an intern you would not get paid.”

Llamas says he now lives and breathes this family-first philosophy himself. The other night Llamas, who now lives in New York, anchored from the World Cup in Los Angeles and went to the game. “But then that same night, I jumped on a red eye so I could be home for a 9 AM little league game, and that's not something that that anyone has to ask me for — that's something I want to do, because I just believe that that kind of stuff needs to be automatic.”

This Father’s Day, Llamas has a message for all the dads out there: “It is the best job in the world to be a father [but] give yourself some grace cause it's really tough out there. There's a lot of books and opinions and podcasts and all kinds of things that are trying to tell people how to [parent] and I think, you know, just enjoy your time with your kids. Because it goes by very fast, and I truly think the greatest thing in the world is to be a dad.”

#7983. As A Therapist, I Thought Caregiver Burnout Wouldn’t Come For Me. I Was Wrong.

The sandwich generation is sorely lacking in support.

Tuesday, 8:10 p.m. I’m helping my 87-year-old mother brush her teeth and change for bed. My 10-year-old calls from the room next door that he and his dad are done reading his latest Big Nate book. He asks (again) when I’m coming to his room to say goodnight. I try not to rush my mother, but I’m exhausted after a long day, and keenly aware of missing those precious minutes right before bedtime when you get the real deal from your child about everything that happened that day.

After months of juggling my work as a therapist with caring for my aging mother (who has been diagnosed with dementia), and being a present, engaged mom and wife, I had to admit that I was dropping some balls. Having all of this on my plate was clearly not working.

I knew I was not alone — I’ve been having this conversation with many friends and clients, also in their 40s or early 50s. In fact, 47% of caregivers under the age of 50 are part of the sandwich generation, those of us who are raising children and caring for aging parents at the same time. If we aren't talking about perimenopause with all its patches and pills, we’re talking about the health concerns of our parents and, potentially, our grandparents as well.

The burnout I was feeling falls particularly heavily on the shoulders of women. Even if you have siblings, most of the caregiving responsibility consistently falls on one person, and that person is typically a woman. Women shoulder the majority of caregiving responsibilities, often to the detriment of their careers. To make matters worse, some caregivers may have a complicated relationship with the parent who is now dependent on them.

Caring for your parent can be immensely rewarding and depressing. Sometimes I feel deeply honored to care for the person who dedicated her life to caring for me. Other times, my mom can’t remember why her beloved husband hasn’t come home yet — my father passed away several years ago. She really doesn’t enjoy having to be bathed by her child, for that matter.

As a mental health professional who has sat with clients going through this very thing, I expected to have more of the answers, to be able to cope and balance more than someone else due to my experience. But the truth is, nothing can truly prepare you for your induction into the sandwich generation.

No matter how we try to overcome the difficulty of caregiving as individuals, we must acknowledge that there’s minimal financial or systemic help for consistent care for the elderly living at home. Some Medicare programs can provide all your healthcare in one place, which is obviously better than driving all over town talking to doctors who aren’t talking to each other. But they often only offer last-minute daily help and, because of the high need in our country, you typically see a new caregiver each day. While better than nothing, it’s clearly not a great situation for a parent who is already confused in their day-to-day life. Some programs actually pay you, the caregiver, for your work, but that doesn’t give you back the missed moments with your own children or restore those career opportunities.

Eventually my husband and I realized that we needed help. Fortunately, we could afford to pay a nurse out of pocket, but the costs have been steep: tens of thousands of dollars annually to have carers for my mother seven days a week, and that’s with me still doing bedtime duty on the weekends. It’s simply not realistic or sustainable for most people.

And one of the challenges that we don’t often talk about is the guilt. Even if you are able to defy the odds and pay someone to come in to help, you still feel guilty about it and get caught up in the “shoulds.” I should be able to care for my parents and my children at the same time; people have been doing this forever with a lot less help. I should be grateful to be able to spend whatever time I have left with my parent. The important part missing from that is the fact that many of us don’t have villages in the way we used to — that nearby family network that would support each other during all the stages of life.

Our lack of a village came into focus for me recently when we adopted a baby into our family. She has brought us more joy than we could have imagined, and I see how much a community would change this experience for us. In my Mommy and Me classes, so many of the young mothers have discussed having their parents come and stay with them during the early weeks of having a newborn. What a stark contrast for me as a mother, in a different phase in my life, where I am taking care of my parent, rather than her taking care of me and my children.

This is a problem that is not going anywhere. Around the country and the world, people are making tough decisions every day — draining bank accounts, missing out on kids’ milestones, declining promotions and date nights with their partner — to take care of a loved one. The physical, financial, and emotional toll can cause extensive damage to the caregiver’s well-being in so many ways.

We also know what to do about this problem. Studies show that while caregiver burnout is a worldwide issue, it is less so in the countries where (surprise, surprise) there is a strong public healthcare system, flexible work environments for caregivers, and affordable private health insurance. These kinds of safeguards can be a key part of rebuilding a new kind of village and community support. The answer is there. The question is if we will take heed before we all burn out.

Dr. Patrice Le Goy is a licensed marriage and family therapist and international psychologist. She is also the research chair of Maternal Mental Health Now and the board chair of Open Paths Counseling Center, as well as the host of Like-Minded with Dr. Patrice, an award-winning mental health podcast.

Patrice lives in Los Angeles with her husband, two children, and their massive dog who is definitely part wolf. You can follow her on social media @drpatricelegoy.

#7981. 35 Back-To-School Sports Gear Essentials Every Young Athlete Needs

From activewear to snacks to the crucial stuff we all forget about, here’s your complete product guide to the gear your young athlete needs.

Back-to-school season does not just mean notebooks, lunch boxes, and the shoes your kid insists everyone else already has. If your kid plays sports, it also means damp socks wedged into the back seat, a gym bag that smells like evidence, water bottles with no lids, and a towel that is wet, rank, and somehow still in use.

Most young athletes need the same basic stuff, no matter what they play: a sturdy water bottle, sweat-ready clothes, socks that do not quit, sunscreen, towels, deodorant, recovery gear, and something to contain the mess. Nothing here is precious. Nothing is so sport-specific that it only works for one season. This is the Amazon gear parents end up buying anyway, pulled together before the season takes over the sports bag, the laundry room, and your will to live.

A good water bottle is the first thing every young athlete needs, and the first thing they will leave on a bench somewhere. Look for one that is durable, easy to clean, and big enough to get them through practice.

The 50-ounce size gives kids enough water for long practices and tournament days, and the tethered leakproof cap means one less loose lid rolling around the car. It is also lightweight, clippable, and dishwasher-safe, which matters because no parent needs another thing that requires special handling.

Some practices are long, hot, and sweaty enough that water alone may not cut it. A sports drink can help replace electrolytes when sweat is doing most of the work.

This variety pack has electrolytes, with no added sugar and no artificial sweeteners, flavors, or dyes. At 20 calories per bottle, it is a lighter sports-drink option for parents who want hydration help without sending a kid into practice with something that looks like melted candy.

Some sports days run straight through the normal eating schedule, which is how kids end up starving in the car and furious at everyone. A protein bar is useful before practice, after practice, or between games, but check school rules and allergens before tossing one into a team bag.

This 10-count variety pack has flavors built around chocolate, peanut butter, blueberry, fruit, and nuts. The bars are gluten-free, made with simple ingredients, and have 12 grams of protein per bar, but some contain common allergens including eggs, peanuts, almonds, and cashews.

Fall sports still mean sun exposure. A sweat-resistant sunscreen belongs in every sports bag, especially for after-school practices, weekend tournaments and kids who swear they “don’t burn.”

This sunscreen is fast-absorbing, nongreasy, and water- and sweat-resistant for up to 80 minutes, which makes it a practical fit for practices and games. Supergoop is made for face and body, so kids do not need separate bottles.

A school backpack is already doing too much. A dedicated sports bag gives clothes, towels, water bottles, deodorant, and gear somewhere to live that is not the floor of your car.

This has a spacious main compartment for school and practice gear, plus a ventilated shoe compartment to keep wet sneakers or cleats away from clean clothes and tech. The water-resistant base is the quiet win here, because locker room floors, wet fields, and rainy parking lots are not kind to regular backpacks.

Wet socks, damp towels, and postpractice clothes should not touch anything clean. A wet-dry bag keeps the gross stuff contained until someone remembers laundry exists.

These bags are technically built for diapers, swimsuits, and day care messes, which is exactly why it works for youth sports. The 12.5-by-16-inch size, washable fabric, heat-sealed seams, and leak-resistant design make it useful for wet socks, damp towels, and gear you do not want touching anything else.

Cotton is fine until it turns into a wet dish towel with sleeves. A moisture-wicking shirt helps kids stay more comfortable through practice, conditioning, and the ride home.

The quick-drying fabric wicks sweat and dries fast, which is the whole point of a practice shirt. It is soft enough for school or general wear too, so it does not become another piece of gear that only gets used once a week.

Every young athlete needs shorts that can handle sweat, dirt, turf, and repeated washing. They should be light, easy to move in, and not so expensive that losing one pair becomes a family event.

The listing calls these soccer shorts, but the sweat-wicking Climacool fabric, adjustable drawcord waist, and recycled polyester interlock make them useful for more than one sport. They are built for movement and repeated washing, which is what matters.

Bad underwear can ruin a practice faster than bad weather. Athletic underwear should move, breathe, and stay put under uniforms, shorts, and base layers without bunching, pinching, or becoming the thing your kid complains about the entire ride home.

These have a 5-inch inseam, a wide soft waistband, a breathable athletic feel, and flatlock seams for durability. The contoured pouch and tagless back make them a practical under-uniform option for boys who need support without bulk.

These are made with smooth stretch fabric, a seamless waistband, and a tag-free design to help reduce irritation during school, sports, and everyday movement. The lightweight performance fabric gives active kids a flexible fit without pinching, digging, or bunching under gear.

A hoodie is the unofficial uniform of kids waiting before games, riding home after practice, or denying they are cold.

This is a straightforward school-to-practice hoodie with a relaxed fit, kangaroo pocket, thumbholes, and midweight fabric. It is the kind of layer kids can wear constantly without making you nervous every time it leaves the house.

A base layer helps with sweat, coverage, and comfort without adding bulk. It works under jerseys, hoodies, and uniforms when the weather cannot decide to be seasonally appropriate.

This long-sleeve top is made with lightweight HeatGear fabric that wicks sweat and dries fast, with mesh panels for ventilation and flatlock seams for easier movement. It is not a heavy thermal layer, but that is why it works for school sports: Kids can wear it under gear without overheating five minutes into warm-ups.

Socks disappear faster than almost anything else in a young athlete’s life. Buy more than seems reasonable, because wet, thin, or blister-making socks can wreck a practice fast.

These socks use a combed cotton and polyester blend with spandex for stretch, which means they are built to breathe, hold their shape, and survive repeated washing. The medium cushioning and reinforced heels and toes make them a practical everyday pick for kids who burn through socks like it is part of the sport.

Slides give kids something easy to wear before and after games, especially when cleats are muddy, socks are wet, or feet need a break. They also make locker rooms, pools, and postpractice errands less gross.

These slides use OOfoam, which the brand says absorbs 37% more impact than traditional footwear foams. The closed-cell foam is machine-washable and designed to minimize odor, which makes it perfect for locker rooms, postgame errands, and the ride home.

A quick-dry towel works for sweat, rain, swimming, muddy legs, and the towel situation no parent wants to inspect. It dries faster than a regular bath towel, which matters when it gets forgotten in a bag overnight.

The listing says it absorbs five times its own weight and dries fast when hung by the snap loop. It also packs into a ventilated carry bag, which makes it easier to keep in a sports bag than a bulky bath towel from home.

A sports bag becomes a swamp fast. Packing cubes give clean clothes, extra socks, base layers, and small gear a fighting chance of staying together instead of becoming part of the bottom-of-the-bag sludge.

These packing cubes keep clean backup clothes, socks, and small gear organized inside a sports bag, backpack or a duffel. The Del Dia colors are random and one-of-a-kind, which means no two sets look the same, and your kid has a chance — albeit small — of recognizing their own stuff.

Youth sports shoes can turn toxic fast, especially when they live in a bag between practices. A shoe deodorizer helps keep sneakers, cleats, and slides from stinking up the car, mudroom, or whatever corner your kid has claimed for gear.

These compact deodorizers are built for shoes, gym bags, lockers, and sports gear, so they do not just solve one stink problem. The twist-to-activate design lets kids control the scent level, assuming they remember to use these before the shoes become a family issue.

Some sports smells do not come out in the wash because the offending item never goes in the wash. A gear spray helps with helmets, gloves, pads, bags, and other equipment that gets sweaty, rank, and somehow keeps getting used.

This spray deodorizes sports equipment, including helmets, gloves, bags, pads and gym gear, and the brand says it works for everything from football and hockey to lacrosse, soccer, volleyball, and boxing. It only requires a spray-and-air-dry routine, which is about as much cleaning as most sports families can promise on a weeknight.

Keep one in the sports bag, one at home, and maybe one in the car, because youth sports have a way of exposing every deodorant failure.

This deodorant is dermatologically tested and made for young, sensitive skin, which makes sense for kids who are just starting to need it. It is designed to protect against body odor without using a grown-up scent that announces itself from across the room.

Sometimes there is no shower. Body wipes help kids clean up enough to survive the car ride, dinner, homework or whatever comes next.

These individually wrapped 8-by-10-inch wipes are made for the exact no-shower problem sports families know well. They are hypoallergenic, paraben-free, and alcohol-free, and include aloe vera and vitamin E, so they are a practical bag staple for postpractice cleanup.

Fields, gyms, locker rooms, and portable bathrooms are not exactly sterile environments. Hand sanitizer is small, cheap, and useful before snacks, after bathroom runs, and after handling shared gear.

This unscented trio gives you three travel-friendly sanitizer sprays, which is useful if you want one for the sports bag, one for the car, and one that will disappear immediately.

Sunscreen, deodorant, lip balm, wipes, hair ties, and sanitizer should not be rolling loose at the bottom of a sports bag. A small toiletry bag keeps the tiny essentials together and makes them easier to find

This zip pouch has internal mesh pockets and a separate compartment, so the small stuff has a fighting chance of staying organized. The swivel hook is useful for hanging it in a locker, on a backpack or anywhere that is not the bottom of a filthy sports bag.

Lips burn too, and kids almost never think about it. SPF lip balm is small enough to live in a bag and useful for long days outside.

This three-pack has SPF 30 and includes aloe and vitamin E to help protect and moisturize lips. The multi-pack is useful because lip balm has the life expectancy of a loose sock.

Late-summer and fall practices can come with mosquitoes, especially on fields near grass, water, or woods. Bug spray keeps kids from spending half of practice swatting instead of playing.

This spray repels mosquitoes, ticks, and biting flies, and the misting design gives more even coverage than the panic-spray method most kids use.

Hair ties vanish, break, and somehow become community property. Keep extras in the sports bag for any kid who needs hair out of their face, whether they play rec soccer or want to look like Norway’s Erling Haaland before warm-ups.

These hair ties are designed to flex with different hair thicknesses and hold without pinching or pulling. They are also made to minimize breakage, which matters when a kid is ripping out a ponytail in the car after practice.

Fall sports do not stop because the weather is annoying. A lightweight rain jacket gives kids real coverage for wet practices, sidelines, and the long walk from field to car.

This waterproof nylon shell is light enough to layer but protective enough for everything from drizzle to a sudden downpour. It has a hood, two hand pockets, elastic cuffs, and reflective detail, which makes it a practical all-season piece for kids who will absolutely claim they are fine while visibly getting soaked.

Something will hurt. A reusable ice pack is useful for bumps, sore knees, rolled ankles, and the ride home after a hard practice.

These reusable gel packs stay flexible out of the freezer, so they can wrap around knees, ankles and other hard-to-ice spots. The included soft cover adds a barrier between the cold pack and skin, which makes it easier to use in the car or on the couch after practice.

Reusable ice packs only help if someone remembered the freezer. Instant cold packs belong in a sports bag or tournament kit for away games and minor sideline injuries.

These single-use cold packs activate after folding, so parents do not need a freezer, cooler, or advance planning to get cold therapy on the sideline. They are designed to reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit, which is exactly the point.

Athletic tape is the thing nobody thinks about until someone needs it immediately. It can help with sore knees, cranky ankles, tight shoulders and small body complaints that show up five minutes before warmups.

This 16-foot roll can be cut to size, so parents are not locked into one strip length for every kid, joint, or complaint. It is breathable, hypoallergenic, and latex-free, and it’s designed to stay on for one to three days through sweat, showers, and weather, while still allowing a range of motion.

New shoes, wet socks, and long tournament days can turn a small hot spot into a full limp. Blister bandages take up almost no room and can save a practice, game or long ride home.

These hydrocolloid bandages cushion blisters, cuts, and scrapes while helping protect them from water, dirt and germs. They are waterproof and designed to stay on for up to five days, which is useful when a kid’s heel is already angry and the season has no interest in pausing.

Youth sports produces scrapes, turf burns, mystery cuts, and dramatic reactions to minor blood. A small first-aid kit should have bandages, antiseptic wipes, gauze, and the basics you need before anyone starts searching the glove compartment for a napkin.

This compact hardcase packs 120 supplies, including adhesive bandages, butterfly closures, gauze pads, alcohol prep pads, antiseptic wipes, sting relief pads, gloves, tweezers, scissors, and medical tape. It is slim enough to fit in a backpack, glove box, or sports bag, but stocked well enough for the everyday cuts, scrapes, and minor injuries that come with kids playing hard.

This is the most sport-specific item on the list. It matters for football, lacrosse, field hockey, basketball, martial arts, wrestling, and other sports in which player contact, falls, elbows, or sticks can impact teeth.

This boil-and-bite mouthguard molds to the teeth for a more custom fit and is made with shock-absorbing EVA material to help protect teeth, gums, and jaw during contact sports. The slim profile, airflow vents, and optional strap version make it more practical for kids who need protection but still have to breathe, talk, and keep it in place.

If it is not labeled, it is a donation to the lost-and-found economy. Name labels help water bottles, hoodies, towels, bags, shoes, and gear make their way back before another parent takes home the same black sweatshirt.

This 114-label pack includes stick-on clothing labels, shoe labels, large and small rectangle labels, and bag tags, so parents can mark almost everything that leaves the house. The labels are peel-and-stick, waterproof and laundry-safe, which matters when the gear is sweaty, wet, washed constantly, or lost somewhere between the field and the car.

Long practices, races, meets, and tournament days can turn kids into empty tanks fast. Energy chews are quick, portable fuel for older kids who need carbs they can eat fast without digging through a bag for whatever got crushed at the bottom.

These chews have 23 grams of carbs per serving. They are organic, include sodium to help replenish electrolytes after exercise, and are easier to stash in a gym bag than a full-size snack.

Warm-up pants used to mean joggers, but kids have moved on. Wide-leg sweatpants are the more current version: loose; comfortable; and useful before practice, after practice, or on the ride home.

These have an elastic waist, pockets, and a wide-leg cut that feels more current than basic warm-ups. The fabric is lightweight, soft, breathable, and slightly stretchy, which makes these useful for school, practice, running around, and the postgame outfit change your kid suddenly cares about.

These have a straight, wide-leg cut, letter print, and loose, trendy fit that works with hoodies, jackets and sweatshirts. They are made for daily wear, workouts, sports, running, and outdoor activities, which puts them in the exact lane between warm-up pants and “my kid will actually wear these.”

This is not performance gear. This is for the kid who walks off the field sweaty, red-faced, and suddenly needs to fix their hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot.

This sea salt spray is made to add volume, shine, and gritty texture without the crunch. It adds grip before styling, which should help with the sacred ritual of fixing the hair before anyone is allowed to leave the parking lot. Postgame vanity is real, and frankly, it may be the most consistent part of youth sports.

Yellowing leaves this month are usually caused by the #1 seasonal mistake houseplant parents make. Here’s how to save your plant's life before it’s too late.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your houseplant leaves are turning yellow this November, your plant is sending urgent distress signals that you really need to heed. As days shorten and sunlight becomes less intense in fall, most houseplants use far less moisture as their growth dramatically slows. Continuing your summer watering routine during this shift creates waterlogged soil, quickly leading to root rot – and an avoidable trip to the compost bin. Catch that first yellow leaf early, however, and you can quickly reverse the damage to keep your houseplant happy and healthy.

Failing to adjust a watering routine in line with houseplants’ seasonal needs is the most common mistake we plant parents make, and unfortunately the root rot that results can be fatal. It takes a few weeks of waterlogged soil and rotting roots before the damage manifests with yellowing leaves, which is why this symptom usually shows up in November – and why once you spot a yellowing leaf you need to take swift action.

So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a yellowing leaf, and save it from an untimely death with a simple fix.

Take a closer look at the yellow houseplant leaf to see what tone, shape, position and extent of the discoloration is. Different plants show this early symptom of root rot in various ways: a Monstera will likely get a yellow halo on one of its monster-sized leaves while a ZZ plant leaf will turn bright yellow from top to bottom overnight. Peperomia foliage typically fades to a pale yellow while a snake plant leaf takes on a translucent yellow tone at the base. Matching up the symptoms to the plant species is a surefire way to tell if overwatering is the cause.

Match your houseplant to the symptoms and you have your diagnosis.

Large, thin-leafed tropical plants like monstera, calathea, anthurium and clumping philodendron typically show a bright yellow halo around a dark spot from overwatering. This happens because as roots begin to rot in soggy soil, fungal or bacterial pathogens in the potting mix travel up the plant and into the leaf tissue. Dead leaf cells show up as a black or brown area, and the bright ring of yellow around it is where the plant is attempting to stop the infection spreading.

ZZ plants (Zamioculcas zamiifolia), caladiums, and elephant ears (Alocasia and Colocasia) grow from potato-like rhizomes or tubers that store lots of water, so it can take these plants a little longer to show signs of overwatering. When they do, it's dramatic though! If these houseplants receive more water than they can process and rot sets in, nutrients are suddenly cut to a whole stem. The entire stalk and its foliage will quickly drain of color to turn a solid strong yellow, top to bottom.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Prayer plants (Maranta), peperomia, Chinese money plants (Pilea peperomioides), African violets (Saintpaulia), nerve plants (Fittonia) and Boston and maidenhair ferns all have a shallow network of very fine, fragile roots. Suffocating in overwatered soil, these thin roots quickly disintegrate and the leaves lose their lustre then become limp and fade through pale green to a matte yellow. Don’t expect these leaves to be mushy from all that water: because the root damage cuts the water supply off, leaves will become dry and brittle, snapping off immediately when touched or simply dropping from the plant.

Jade plants (Crassula ovata), snake plants, Christmas or Thanksgiving cacti (Schlumbergera), echeverias and aloe vera all store water in their stems or leaves, and excess moisture causes them to turn a translucent, sickly yellow at the base. The area will also feel mushy and this may happen where stems or leaves meet the soil, in which case stems may topple over, but also where leaves attach to stems or leaf segments join together.

Vining plants like pothos (Epipremnum aureum), English ivy (Hedera helix), wax plants (Hoya) and heartleaf philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) typically show overwatering symptoms on their oldest leaves near the base first. Unable to draw as many nutrients through suffocating roots, the plant strips nutrients from its older, less productive leaves to feed the fresh growth at its tips in the hope of finding a more suitable environment. Stripped of chlorophyll, the base foliage turns an even, uniform yellow while the newer growth at the stem tip remains green.

Overwatered houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants (Chlorophytum comosum) and ponytail palms (Beaucarnea recurvata) typically develop brown foliage tips with a yellow area separating them from the healthy green tissue. This happens because the leaf tips are at the very end of the plant's plumbing system so, when roots are damaged and can't take up water effectively, are the first to run out of moisture. The yellow color below the dead brown leaf tissue is the plant trying to salvage what nutrients it can. The leaves may lose their upright arch and start to droop, too.

If you spot yellowing houseplant leaves, immediately stop watering and let the soil dry out. Slide the pot off and if you see white roots, you’ve caught the problem in time. Pop the plant back into its pot and only water when the top inch of potting mix feels dry. A moisture meter like this from Amazon takes out the guesswork and helps you adjust your routine to the plant's fluctuating needs going forwards, and water houseplants properly.

If there’s a foul, stagnant smell, however faint, and roots look dark, root rot has set in and you’ll need to take action to save your plant. Remove as much soil as possible and use sharp scissors or pruners or to snip off all roots that look dark or feel mushy or slimy. Rinse the roots and wash the pot, then repot your houseplant.

It's vital the pot has a drainage hole so excess moisture can escape (and a saucer to save your surfaces). If you adore a decorative hole-less pot, use it as a cachepot with a holed plastic pot inside. For succulent plants that store water in their leaves or stems, fill your pot with a fast-draining potting mix like Back to the Roots Organic Succulents & Cacti Mix, available from The Home Depot. For everything else, use an indoor potting mix with coconut coir and perlite that evens out moisture levels while allowing good drainage like Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix For All Plants, available from Walmart.

Upgrade your irrigation with a watering can that has a long, gooseneck spout like this indoor can from Walmart for more precise, controlled water delivery.

Every week, the Garden ER series brings you simple solutions to this season's most pressing problems, for happy and healthy plants without any hassle.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. #7979. My Parents Took Me Voting. Now I'm Doing The Same With My Daughter.

Your candidate might not always win. But, as my parents taught me, it’s important to show up anyway.

My earliest memories of voting take place at the elementary school up the street from my parents’ house. Every Election Day, my parents would bring me and my younger sister along with them to the polls. I remember standing in the long lines impatiently wondering when it’d be our turn. I remember at least one year where there was a mock ballot for kids. And, perhaps most importantly to elementary-school-aged me, I remember receiving the prized Future Voter sticker at the end.

At the time, I didn’t think of any of this as civic education. My parents weren’t necessarily sitting us down for lectures about democracy or giving us pop quizzes on the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (although that would come later during my AP U.S. Government class). My parents were simply voting and we were watching. But, as it turns out, we were learning by observing.

My parents made it abundantly clear to my sister and me that voting was both a right and a responsibility — and that this wasn’t always the case for people who looked like us. As Black girls growing up in America, that history mattered. We learned that Black people had marched, organized, been beaten and even killed for the right my parents exercised so routinely at the elementary school around the corner.

So, when Election Day came around, we went. And not just for the presidential elections every four years. My parents participated in every election — local, federal, didn’t matter. The responsibility was the same.

By the time I was finally old enough to vote myself, I couldn’t wait.

I missed being able to vote in the 2004 presidential election by a year, which meant the 2008 election would be my first chance to vote for president. And I felt elated that my first presidential vote would be for the country’s first Black president.

At the time, I was working as a reporter at my community newspaper in a conservative county in Maryland. On Election Day, a colleague and I spent hours driving around to various polling places, interviewing voters and reporting on turnout before returning to the Board of Elections to wait for results.

After work, I went home and watched the national returns with my dad. When Barack Obama walked onto the stage in Chicago’s Grant Park with his beautiful Black family, I remember staring at the television in disbelief.

Wow, I thought to myself, soaking in the moment. I just witnessed history.

But elections don’t always end with the history you hoped to witness.

In 2016, I proudly cast my ballot for Hillary Clinton and went to bed believing we were about the elect the country’s first woman president. We all know how that turned out.

Four years later, I voted for Joe Biden, but I was especially excited about his running mate, Kamala Harris, whom I’d supported in the Democratic primary. Watching a Black and Asian woman become vice president meant something different to me. Of course, representation isn’t the only reason to vote for someone and I think we’re all doing ourselves a disservice if we pretend as if identity is entirely separate from politics. As a Black woman in America, I’d spent most of my life looking at the highest echelons of power and rarely seeing anyone who looks like you.

In the spring of 2024, I picked up my then two-year-old daughter Violet from daycare, went to swim lessons and then swung by our neighborhood elementary school to vote in the Illinois presidential primary. With her little puffs and binky in tow, she naturally became the star of the polling place.

Our next-door neighbor, Mr. Steve, was working the polls that day and gave Violet a Future Voter sticker. She was entranced. To her, the sticker was probably the best part of the whole outing, which, when I thought about it, was exactly how I felt when I was her age (and, let’s be real, is also how I feel as an adult).

Afterward, we went outside to the school playground and, as I watched her run around, it hit me what a full-circle moment this had become. And then I had another thought: This could be a children’s book.

I wanted to write a book that could explain voting to children around Violet’s age: something that would talk about walking into a polling place; why grown-ups stood in line to fill out ballots; what even is a ballot; and why any of this matters anyway.

That fateful afternoon eventually became the premise of Violet Goes Voting, an early reader about a little girl accompanying her parents to the polls and learning that voting is one way we use our voices. But the book was just the beginning.

That fall, my husband and I took Violet with us when we voted in the presidential election. This time, I had a very specific picture in my head of what the moment might look like in both real life and the book version. My daughter would sit on my lap as I cast my ballot to elect the first Black woman president of the United States.

My parents had taken their Black daughters to the polls so we would understand that our voices mattered. Decades later, I would take mine with me as I helped elect a Black woman to the White House. Except, of course, that’s not what happened.

Like so many people, I woke up the next morning devastated. The history I had imagined sharing with my daughter would have to wait. Since then, I’ve thought a lot about what, exactly, I want Violet to inherit from me and learn from all of this.

Because maybe the lesson was never supposed to be that if you show up, your candidate will win. My parents certainly never promised that to me. What they taught me was the importance of showing up anyway.

Voting is a small part of civic engagement, but it was my introduction to it nonetheless. Long before I knew what a primary was, before I understood the harsh reality of voter suppression or could name any of my congressional representatives, before I was old enough to fill in a bubble next to a candidate’s name, I knew what Election Day looked like.

It looked like my parents making time to go to the polls. It looked like my sister and me eagerly tagging along. It looked like waiting our turn. And, yes, it looked like getting a sticker at the end.

Now, as a mom, I understand that those seemingly ordinary trips were teaching me something much bigger: This is what our family does. We show up. We pay attention. We responsibly exercise the rights people before us fought to secure. We don’t take them for granted.

Only time will tell who Violet will vote for when she’s old enough to cast her first ballot. And, frankly, we have a while before that happens. She’s much more interested in playgrounds than politics at the moment, which is exactly how it should be for an innocent five-year-old.

But I hope that when her first Election Day arrives, she’ll look back on our family selfie from outside the voting place in 2024. I hope she’ll remember me reading to her the book that she inspired. I hope she understands why walking into that booth and making her own choice carries a history older than the both of us combined.

But most of all and most importantly, I simply hope she shows up. Because that’s the inheritance my parents gave me and my sister. And now it’s mine to pass on.

L’Oreal Thompson Payton is an author, journalist and the founder of Zora’s Place, a Black feminist bookstore and community hub in Evanston, Illinois. Her books include Stop Waiting for Perfect, Amanda Gorman: Poet and Activist, Violet Goes Voting and the highly-anticipated memoir Infertile Black Girl (Fall 2027). Her byline has appeared in outlets such as Essence, Fortune, New York magazine and SELF. Learn more at lorealthompsonpayton.com.

#7978. 10 Times Ted Lasso Totally Nailed This Whole Parenting Thing

Ted Lasso isn’t the perfect father, but he’s one who can teach us a thing... or 10.

Way back in 2020, when I heard that Apple TV was releasing a Ted Lasso show based on the NBC Sports English Premier League promo campaign of the same name, I dismissed the concept out of hand. Sure, I loved the cheeky ads where an American football coach goes to England to manage a football club. But the premise felt too thin to flesh out into a full series, and Jason Sudeikis’ body of work up to that point didn’t inspire confidence that a sitcom based on the character could hold my attention.

Here’s the thing I failed to anticipate: Ted Lasso is, at its core, a show about fatherhood. Not in a neat, Hallmark-movie kind of way, but in the messy, long-distance, guilt-soaked, love-you-so-much-it-hurts way that a lot of us actually live it. Ted’s relationship with his son, Henry — conducted mostly through grainy FaceTime calls across a six-hour time difference — is the quiet beating heart of all three seasons.

While the rest of AFC Richmond is arguing about formations and tabloid covers, Ted is trying to figure out how to be a good dad from 4,000 miles away while working through how his relationship with his own father has formed him.

The man is not perfect. Nobody raising kids is, and running off to London without your family to accept a job you’re wholly unqualified for as an act of emotional avoidance is a narrative necessity, but it’s a flaw many folks have pointed out.

But along the way, he does his best and makes the right plays in the moments that count. And since parenting lessons wrapped inside a feel-good soccer comedy are my personal favorite delivery mechanism, let’s run through 10 times Ted Lasso gave us a genuine master class in this whole dad thing.

It’s Ted’s first night in London. He’s jet-lagged and disoriented, and the very first thing he does is call home to Henry. He fumbles the time zones and sounds a little lost, but he makes sure his kid hears his voice before the day is out.

There’s a version of Ted Lasso in a different corner of the multiverse who gets swept up in the new job, the new city, the chaos of it all, and phones it in on the fatherhood front. This Ted doesn’t. He knows that presence isn’t always physical. Sometimes it’s a crackling FaceTime connection at midnight your time, 6 a.m. their time, just so your kid knows you’re still there.

Henry, during a video call, asks his dad if he’s ever run into The Beatles over there in England and whether he can get a photo with John, Paul, George, and Ringo. Now, Ted knows that both John Lennon and George Harrison have been dead for decades. He also knows his kid is 8 years old and asking with complete, genuine wonder. So Ted just agrees to try. He doesn't have the heart to kill that particular joy right now.

This one is subtle, but it matters. There's a real parenting skill in knowing when the truth can wait five minutes and when it needs to be delivered immediately. Ted isn't being dishonest — he's being developmentally attuned. There's a season for everything, as a certain king once sang from the stage of a Broadway house, and this particular season called for letting a little kid's imagination breathe. Ted will level with Henry about the hard stuff — and he does, plenty of times — but he picks his moments. That's wisdom.

When Michelle and Henry show up in London, Ted drops everything. They swing by the Crown and Anchor for an authentic English pub experience. They build a double-decker bus model at the kitchen table. And Henry settles into his happy place, sleeping between his parents. Even though Ted is in the midst of a brutal season, managing a locker room full of fragile egos while racking up losses, none of that matters for those few days. He is simply Dad.

What makes this moment rich is what we know that Henry doesn't: His parents' marriage is already over. Michelle is about to tell Ted she wants a divorce. And yet Ted keeps the joy intact for his son. He doesn't let his own grief occupy the visit. That is an act of real parenting discipline — the ability to compartmentalize your own pain long enough to give your child a memory that isn't shadowed by yours. Most of us have had to do some version of this. It doesn't feel heroic in the moment. It just feels hard. Ted does it anyway.

Henry asks Ted why, whenever he sees him on TV coaching soccer, he never seems to be doing anything. It's a kid's question, but it's actually a perfect question. Ted's answer is one of the most quietly profound things in the entire series. He tells Henry that once the game starts, he can't really tell his players what to do — he just has to hope that everything he's been trying to teach them made some kind of dent. Then he says: “It's kind of like being a father.”

And then Henry, having absorbed none of this, is clearly already thinking about something else entirely. Ted realizes midsentence that his kid has mentally bounced. He stops talking. He smiles. He gets it. That moment is the whole job description of parenthood distilled into 30 seconds of television. You pour yourself into the role and hope it lands. You accept that you can't control the outcome. And you find a way to laugh about it — or at least smile — when your kid demonstrates, in real time, that they were not listening. Every parent reading this has lived this exact moment.

Henry isn’t the first kid to idolize a less-than-stellar role model, but his admiration for Jamie Tartt is a particular form of torture for Ted. As enigmatic as he is talented, Jamie makes Ted’s life incredibly difficult, even when he’s scoring goals. This puts Ted in a tough spot as Henry enthusiastically belts out the terribly annoying Baby Shark-themed Jamie Tartt song and sports his jersey with pride.

But Ted lets his son revel in the moment of having access to the talented and popular starlet. He doesn’t even hint at the fact that perhaps Tartt isn’t the best guy to look up to. And when Jamie flashes Ted a smirk that makes his beautiful face even more punchable than usual while signing Henry’s jersey, Ted takes a deep breath and lets his son have a moment he’ll never forget.

Ted gets word from Michelle that Henry has been involved in a bullying situation at school — and then discovers it wasn't Henry who was bullied. Henry was the bully. Ted is shaken. And because of schedules and time zones, he has difficulty getting in touch with Henry right away.

If Ted had been around, he would likely have responded emotionally and sucked all the air out of the room. But when father and son finally get a chance to talk, Henry admits he messed up and didn't follow his dad's advice to count to 10 when he gets angry.

With a little bit of forced space, Henry comes back around on his own. Ted doesn't strip his son of dignity while correcting him. And when Henry apologizes to his friend Doug with a rap in front of the class, you can almost hear Ted beaming through the phone. The lesson Ted had been repeating wasn't wasted — it just needed more time to work. Be a goldfish, sure, but also trust that the seeds you plant eventually grow. Even in the hardest soil.

When Michelle and Henry leave London at the end of their visit, Ted walks them to the gate, knowing his marriage is essentially over and that his son doesn't know it. He says goodbye to Henry the way you say goodbye when you're not sure when you'll see each other again — fully present, holding it together, promising to talk soon. He watches Henry walk away with the airport attendant. And then the mask slips, just for a moment, and you see how much it costs him.

Here's what Ted doesn't do: He doesn't make the goodbye about himself. He doesn't get weepy in a way that burdens Henry with having to manage his father's emotions. He saves that for after the kid is out of sight. This is something parents don't talk about enough — the emotional labor of keeping your own grief off your child's plate. It's not suppression. It's protection. There's a version of this that's emotionally avoidant and unhealthy, but Ted's version in this moment is clear-eyed and loving. He feels everything. He just knows whose feelings need managing right now.

After Henry's visit to London ends and the lad heads back to Kansas, Ted does something small and wonderful. He shows Henry, via video call, that he's placed the miniature Premier League Lego trophy Henry gave him into the Nelson Road Stadium Lego set they built together. It's a tiny thing. It's also everything.

Physical objects carry emotional weight for kids in ways that words sometimes can't. That Lego stadium becomes a shared artifact. It’s something Henry can picture when he thinks of his dad. Something that says “you were here, and you matter, and I kept a piece of what we made.”

It's the parenting equivalent of keeping a drawing on the fridge forever. Henry even notices that Nate's Lego figure is at the back of the bench and asks about it, which gives Ted a gentle opening to explain that relationships can change without anyone being erased. Heavy stuff, delivered through the medium of tiny plastic soccer coaches.

During their Lego video call conversation, Ted tells Henry that he doesn't love the idea of being away from him and that the only reason he's staying in England is that he's doing something important. Henry — who is, let's remember, about 10 years old — tells his dad to try to win the whole thing. Ted pushes back, saying winning isn't everything. And Henry says, essentially: “OK, but at least try.”

That's the moment a kid flips the script on you, and you realize they've been absorbing your lessons all along and also developing their own perspective on top of them. Ted doesn't dismiss the advice. He doesn't say “thanks, buddy” in that patronizing way parents sometimes do. He actually sits with it. He lets Henry be right.

Kids need to see their parents receive feedback and adjust — it's how they learn that it's a normal and healthy thing to do. Plus, Henry is objectively correct. You can care about more than winning and still bring your whole effort to the field. That's not a contradiction. That's maturity.

Ted walks away from AFC Richmond. He turns down the job. He gets on the plane. He comes home to Kansas and, within about 60 seconds, is coaching Henry's junior league team, running plays, completely in his element.

But the real parenting lesson isn't just that Ted comes home. It's why he comes home. He doesn't do it because the job went badly or because England rejected him. He does it because he looked at his life clearly and made an honest accounting of what mattered most. He showed his son — showed Henry in the most concrete way possible — that he is the priority. Not in the abstract, inspirational-poster way. In the literal, I-quit-my-dream-job-in-London-to-be-at-your-soccer-games way.

And then in the finale's final image, when Henry misses a shot and gets frustrated, Ted calls him over. Henry says the words Ted has been saying all series — be a goldfish — and they both smile.

The lesson came back home. Same as the dad.

#7977. Musician Allie Teilz says becoming a mom made her “bigger, not smaller”

The DJ’s debut album, Come to Mommy, is a refusal to pick one version of herself, and a reminder that we don’t have to either.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 23, 2026

It’s dinnertime at Allie Teilz’s house, and the music is already on. Perhaps a film score courtesy of Italian classicist Morricone, maybe some Italian disco easing in behind it. One of the twins, age 3, is already dancing to it. The phones go in the ceramic cow on the counter for the remainder of the evening, where her almost-8-year-old likes them. There’s a projector, a record player, and a wall of VHS tapes with Yellow Submarine and The Land Before Time on heavy rotation. Teilz calls it, half-joking, a ’90s-electronics household.

She is, for the record, impossibly cool. A vinyl DJ and producer who came up in Los Angeles nightlife sharing booths with the likes of Grace Jones and Daft Punk, she now scours thrift stores and estate sales for those VHS tapes and describes herself as “a mother first and an artist second.” She is a mother of four who weaves those two versions of herself authentically into one.

We talked for an hour, and I could have gone three more. Somewhere in the course of our call she made me wish, for a second, that I could do the whole motherhood thing over again. My kids are grown and nearly grown, and I am not in the market for a redo. Still, the childhood she is building for hers, steeped in art and music and curiosity, had me calculating.

Her debut album, Come to Mommy, out now, is the sound of her reclaiming the artist within after the babies arrived. It’s atmospheric, irresistibly dance-able and laced with an electronic vibe that’s both throwback and futuristic. The title turns “come to daddy” on its head. The culture asks what Daddy wants. Teilz would rather ask what Mommy wants, and she answers without flinching. “Mommy wants joy,” she says. “She wants to have fun and dance. She wants pleasure and joy.”

Teilz doesn’t treat her kids as the thing she makes art around. She treats them as the reason her art got deeper. “Becoming their mom,” she says, “only made everything bigger, not smaller.” Motherhood taught her that “the deepest creativity can come from having very little time and knowing exactly what matters.”

There’s a surrender in becoming a parent, she says, a soul handing itself over to lead someone else through life, and for her it cracked the work open instead of closing it down. It “liberated me in creation,” she says, and gave her “a deeper well to pull from.” She has taken to calling motherhood “the highest form of art I’ve ever experienced.”

It changed what she wants to make, too. She looks at her own work through her children’s eyes now and holds it to a single north star. What do I want to see more of in the world? Certainly not  “AI art and lobotomy chic,” her encapsulation of the soulless, machine-driven work she’s watched creep in. She wants her kids to have what she had, the feeling of hearing Talking Heads for the first time and being free, the permission to flail around in  an imaginary version of David Byrne’s giant suit and stay in “that beautiful state of play.” Come to Mommy is her attempt to put that feeling back into the world, and she credits her kids as the inspiration. “They’re the greatest teachers,” she says.

Most women are familiar with the shift that happens when you become a mother. The self gets smaller to make room for everyone else, and for a while Teilz felt it, sliding toward the motherhood she’d watched other women vanish into. The mom groups where everyone gave and gave without ever taking their own needs into consideration. The careers set down and never picked back up. The inability to truly answer the question, “Who am I?” She calls out the insidious culprits that get woven into culture. “We’re indoctrinated by The Giving Tree and The Rainbow Fish,” she says, the children’s books that sell self-erasure as generosity. Make yourself a stump and you’ll be loved. Give away your sparkles and you’ll be accepted. “That’s such a dangerous thing,” Teilz observes.

For a long stretch, her own priorities became submerged. What pulled her back was simple. Boundaries. A flip phone for the hours she refuses to be reachable. She points to a line she saw online, “have boundaries or get an autoimmune disorder,” and says that her health was what finally made her stop. “My kids don’t need a mom who disappears into anything,” she says. “Even motherhood.”

Teilz builds her kids’ childhood the way she builds a record, out of specific, deliberate, slightly magical details. When her daughter earned a leader award at school and got to choose the celebration, she asked to make “ice cream mountains” with scoops stacked into a castle on parchment paper, modeled on the shop Teilz loved as a girl. Ridiculous for the sake of being ridiculous. The memories Teilz recalls most fondly from her own childhood aren’t the cruise or the big trip. They’re the one-bedroom apartment and her mom letting the kids pick a favorite ice cream before the first day of school. Now she makes the small, arguably more impactful kind of memories for her own crew.

There’s also a healthy helping of wonder. The kids get sent out to the garden to pull parsley or a tomato so their hands are involved in making dinner–she’s been teaching them to grow things from seed to fruition for years, because watching a baby artichoke push up from a seed you watered is the kind of small miracle she wants them to appreciate. Books work the same way. She still talks about a woman she once watched on the subway, reading beside her small daughter while the car churned around them, the two of them just reading, an image that stuck with her long before she had kids of her own. Now one of her proudest moments is her daughter climbing onto the couch to get lost in Harry Potter. “Stay curious about the world,” she tells other mothers. “Keep reading. Stay interested in what matters to you.”

None of this came easily. Come to Mommy was written through a brutal stretch that included a traumatic birth, one that nearly cost Teilz and one of her sons their lives, and the album is partly the record of her finding the way back. The final track, Back From the Dead, was written for the twin she almost lost. It’s her way of telling all of her kids that they can come back from the worst thing. Making art out of it was a way to process, and she says, proof to her children that you can take something that breaks you and “make something beautiful out of the ashes.”

Near the end, I painted an image for her. A mom pulls into the driveway and sits in the car a minute before going in, the album still playing. What does she want that woman to carry inside with her? Teilz didn’t hesitate. She wants her to “steal the fire” of her own passion, to think of the song she danced hardest to at her best friend’s 13th birthday, to feel held, to have a reason to dance. Mostly she wants her to feel more like herself.

Not many people tell women that the self doesn’t have to shrink to make room for mothering. Teilz spends a whole album saying it.

#7976. Justice Cody Hiland Publicly Criticizes The President For Nominating Him To District Court Instead of Eighth Circuit

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Apparently, the Arkansas Senators are blocking Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination because Hiland didn't get the nomination.

We are coming into the endgame for President Trump's judicial nominees. Since the election, it seems the President has made (at least) two nominations to the federal bench in Texas: Justice James Sullivan of the Texas Supreme Court for the WDTX seat in Austin and OLC Head Elliot Gaiser for the NDTX seat in Dallas. I say "seems" because the President has not posted these nominations to Truth Social, as that makes it official. But the Senate Judiciary Committee has received questionnaires for both candidates. I have known both of these sharp legal minds for some time, and would welcome their addition to the bench. Will Sullivan and Gaiser get votes? I sure hope so. Over the next six weeks, Republican Senators will need to be motived to vote, while Democrat Senators will pull out every stop to leave these seats open. Plus, there is an entire line of other nominees who are still waiting for votes.

Beyond the district court nominees, there is the question of circuit court nominees. Judge Anna St. John's nomination to the Fifth Circuit and Judge Daniel Domenico's nomination to the Tenth Circuit are pending. They had their hearings some time ago, and should get through. Todd Butler has not even had his hearing yet, so he is down the pecking order. Then there is Judge Lee Rudofksy, a nominee to the Eighth Circuit, who had his hearing back in September. Yet, both of the Arkansas Senators are blocking Rudofsky's nomination. Why? They prefer Justice Cody Hiland, a member of the Arkansas Supreme Court.

There's a problem with Hiland. He has demonstrated absolutely terrible judgment which should permanently disqualify him from holding any public office.

In August, he decided to disclose to a room full of law students private communications between him and the White House Counsel. Worse, rather than teaching students about the value of grace, he promoted belligerence and vindictiveness. In short, the White House approached Hiland about a nomination to the Eighth Circuit. After the vetting process, the White House changed course, and offered Hiland a seat on the federal district court. Hiland refused, and told the White House Counsel to tell President Trump about it. He said all of this on a livestream. You can watch it here, starting around the 16:45 mark:

And I've transcribed the comments for those who prefer to read:

The second thing I want to talk about is you're going to have to learn to be resilient, and maybe this far in your career, maybe it's been easy for you. I don't know, but you're going to have to learn how to be knocked down and then get back up, and then also not to be intimidated. Resiliency is something that is going to carry with you the rest of your career. Now, I'm going to tell you a story that just happened to me because resilience matters even at this point in a career. So, you you want to hear a backstory on something? Nobody ever gets to hear backstories. I'm going to give you a backstory. So, about two months ago, I was contacted about being appointed by the president to the Eighth Circuit. Okay, I had senators who asked me to do it. Applied, went to the interview in front of a White House panel of eight Ivy League attorneys, did an interview, and then got a call. And the call said, "You know what? We're going to recommend that the president appoints you to the Eighth Circuit, and so they started a background check. The FBI goes out, and if you've ever served in these capacities, you know that there's a full field investigation that takes place. And select 12 or 13 agents just investigate you for about six weeks. And in this case, they ask them to finish it in two weeks because they wanted to get it done, and so the FBI went out and they talked to over 130 people about me and my life. And when Dean Crawford is talking about social media, you know that sort of thing matters, okay? Because they go back to the time that you're 18 and they talk to everybody you've ever leased from. They tell you they're going to talk to your girlfriends and everybody else. It's like taking a bath with a brillo pad. Okay, good decisions matter as you go along this course, and so it rocked along. And last Tuesday, I had a meeting. Last Wednesday, I had a meeting for three hours with the Department of Justice, finalizing my Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, and it was going to be sent in. And I was told to go home and to expect a phone call from the President of the United States, and to be offered the position. And so I went home and I charged my phone and I called my wife and I said, "You need to come home tonight's the night. We've been through two months of unbelievable minutia of a life that's quite frankly not that interesting. Okay, but I had to have it all, and we had prepared it. It was ready to it was ready to go. And I get a phone call from 202. For those of you don't know, that's Washington D.C. And the man on the other end of the line was not the president of the United States. It was White House Counsel, who, by the way, had recommended that we be chosen. And White House Counsel said the president would like to know if you would be interested in a federal district court position. Eastern District of Arkansas, and I said, "You mean Circuit, Eighth Circuit? No, no, no. Federal District Judge in the Eastern District of Arkansas." And so your mind starts going, "What in the world has happened? What am I hearing?" And so, being belligerent, and at times I said no. That is not a position that I'm interested in. And he came back with after a five second delay of you know not believing what I just said. He said, "So you want me to go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you're rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench, and I said, "Yes, that's exactly what I want you to tell the president of the United States." And so, you know, I tell that story to say this because I want to be honest. Because too many elected officials are just not transparent, and that happened to me last week. You know what? It's okay because I'd never dreamed of being on the Eighth Circuit. It had never been had come to my mind. But we had an expectation based on an FBI investigation, based on communication from those that make these decisions that it was done. And sometimes, guys, it's not done. Sometimes your expectations are not met. When you're a student here with these kind of people, this kind of quality, not everybody is going to make the top paper. Not everybody is going to make law review. Despite what your expectations may be there are times where your expectations are not going to be met, and it's going to happen for the rest of your life at times. And so, as you begin this career, start developing that resiliency.

Talking to law students is my profession. I can't imagine a judge making such a huge blunder. What lesson are these students taking away here? That you should be so stubborn about getting one position that you refuse another lifetime commission? That you should reveal private communications with the White House in which you admit you were "belligerent"? He is comparing not getting an Eighth Circuit appointment to not getting on law review? No wonder the White House didn't pick him. In my view, making a bad nomination is worse than making no nomination at all (see Butler).  The Eighth Circuit is at a turning point. Judge Stras writes far too many dissents. One more vote could flip the circuit. Arkansas is but one state in the circuit. This stubbornness will spite the good people of those states.

Here's the bottom line. Senators pick Judges who are their friends. Those are the worst possible reasons to pick a judge. We need to reward the people who advance the rule of law, not those who are chummy with Senators. And yes, this applies to Todd Butler too. The Junior Senator from Mississippi told people to choose a different protein. Well, they should have chosen a different judge. But here we are.
