#7975. The Busy Mom’s Guide To Gift Shopping On Budget

Amazon and Alexa for Shopping make it easy to get it all for less.

Amazon knows how hard moms are working, and they have some ways to lighten the load. When you shop through Alexa for Shopping — Amazon’s personalized agentic shopping assistant — it all becomes way less stressful and way more affordable, and you might even get enough time back to finish your coffee before it gets cold (can you imagine?).

With everyday low prices that meet or beat other retailers across a huge selection of products, from affordable private-brands that help you save without sacrificing quality to the name-brand finds your kids have been asking for, Amazon makes it easier to find gifts that fit your budget.

Here are a few ways to use Amazon to get all the gifts you need — and stay sane while doing it.

Alexa for Shopping is Amazon’s agentic shopping assistant, and it’s really something else. It combines knowledge of the hundreds of millions of products across Amazon with info from across the web, and applies all of that to your personal shopping history and preferences. In other words, it knows all the possible gifts you could get on Amazon, and it knows you.

You can use Alexa for Shopping by asking it questions, like “What are the best toys for 5 year-olds?” or “What are teenagers asking for this year?” or even “What are some premium and more affordable brand options for a red dress and matching headband for my 3 year-old daughter’s holiday outfit?” It will give you ideas (including taking your shopping history and preferences into account) and then share a list of products to look through. So whether you’re gifting your own kids and just need some fresh ideas when you’re drawing a blank, or shopping for an older niece who lives five states away and have no clue where to start, you get tailored advice that helps you land on the perfect thing.

Budgeting during the holidays is not for the weak. Between finding the perfect gifts for your kids, your mother-in-law, and your spouse, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of holiday shopping and discover more things you know they’ll (or you’ll) love along the way.

The good news? Amazon’s prices consistently meet or beat other retailers, so you’re already getting low, competitive prices when you shop on Amazon. On top of that, Alexa for Shopping is a great tool to help you stay on track. First of all, you can use it so see up to a full year of price history for any product you’re interested in. Once you have that information, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to let you know when it drops to the right price for you. And even better, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to turn on auto-buy so it can complete your purchase using your default payment method when the item reaches your price target.

That saves you time (who has the bandwidth to keep checking back every day?!) and helps you know that when you do hit “buy” (or have Alexa do it for you), you’re getting the thing you want at a great price. And if you do that for all of your holiday shopping, you’re setting yourself up to spend less this season. That can be a huge relief at such an expensive time of year.

Bonus: the savings aren't just about gifts. From stocking up on groceries for the holiday feast to getting extra household essentials for overnight guests, the season comes with plenty of demands. With everyday low prices on fresh groceries and household essentials, plus fast free delivery, you can get the things you need at great prices that help your holiday budget go further.

A large part of the mental mom load is figuring out which [insert kid-related item here] is the best one. From onesies to bikes to pimple patches, there are so many things to choose from, and it takes time to figure out what’s actually right for your kid.

Alexa for Shopping takes that stress off your plate, too. Once you’ve found a few options that might work, Alexa for Shopping’s got you: it can show you side-by-side comparisons, highlighting the differences in features, price points, and even the reviews. Instead of digging through details, you get it all laid out and can quickly make your pick. Goodbye, overthinking.

We all know that holiday magic is really just... moms. But Amazon and the features built into Alexa for Shopping sort of feel like their own kind of magic. With Amazon, you can create a holiday season your kids will always remember, and make it look almost effortless. When you can do that without overspending or screaming into the void? We think that’s beautiful.

(And heads up, the savings go even further with Prime thanks to free delivery, exclusive deals, gas discounts, and more. But we digress.)

The best kind of holiday magic isn't just finding the right gifts at the right prices. It's getting a little time back for yourself, too. And honestly, moms deserve that kind of magic most of all.

Amazon and Prime deliver billions in savings every year — averaging over $1,000 per customer for 100+ million customers. Learn more about how Amazon makes the holidays and everyday life more affordable for families here.

Tulip fire can make your eagerly anticipated spring bulbs look distorted and spotty. But these quick bulb planting checks can help you to prevent calamity later

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Planting some tulips is one of the most enjoyable ways to pass some time this month. It offers the promise of vivid, saturated color to punctuate the winter months. Too often, however, the anticipation can turn to heartbreak, as early leaves emerge stunted, twisted, and scarred with spots. This is classic tulip fire: an aggressive fungal blight that leaves tulips looking as though they were scorched by an open flame.

The frustrating reality of tulip fire is that while symptoms appear in spring, the infection usually begins months earlier during tulip planting. The pathogen enters unnoticed on dry bulb scales, or lies dormant in beds where infected tulips grew before. Once established, no post-planting drench or spray can save infected stems. Your best defense is prevention before your tulip bulbs go in the ground. A few careful checks at planting time give next year's tulips a much better shot. Just a few proactive measures this fall will ensure that your tulips emerge clean, robust, and full of vibrant blooms. Here’s how to address the perils of tulip fire before it ever has a chance to cause problems – so you can look forward to spring with confidence.

Tulip fire is a common tulip disease caused by the fungal pathogen Botrytis tulipae. While closely related to common gray mold (B. cinerea), which attacks soft fruits and perennials, B. tulipae is host-specific and targets tulips almost exclusively. This host specificity is an advantage for gardeners. If you deny the fungus its preferred host for 3-4 seasons, resting populations in the soil gradually starve and decline.

Recognizing early symptoms is key to containment. In early spring, infected bulbs send up stunted, crumpled shoots known as fireheads. These sickly stems become blanketed in fuzzy gray fungal spores that blow or splash onto neighboring plants during cool, rainy weather. Tiny, water-soaked flecks quickly spread across foliage, coalescing into scorched brown blotches, while flower buds rot before opening. Wet spring conditions across USDA hardiness zones 3-8 accelerate spore dispersal, and can turn an isolated infection into an outbreak within a week.

Most cultivated tulip hybrids are at risk in damp, overcrowded conditions. However, species tulips with lower profiles (like Tulipa clusiana or T. tarda) and sturdy Darwin hybrid varieties demonstrate better resilience than dense, double-flowered late types. If you’re still deciding which bulbs to get, try bold Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Amazon for weather resistant stems, and dreamily elegant Salmon Impression Darwin Hybrid Tulip Bulbs from Plant Addicts for natural vigor. Here's how to prevent your tulips turning into fireheads. Grab your bulbs and get ready!

Preventing tulip fire adds only a few minutes to your fall planting routine, but the benefits are immeasurable. Proactive defense focuses on basic cultural care: thoughtful checks, site and timing prep, and ample airflow. The following simple checks take just a little extra preparation, providing peace of mind and protecting your spring displays long before the first green shoots pierce the soil…

Before planting your bulbs, empty your bulb bags onto an outdoor potting bench or table, and inspect each one individually. A healthy, viable tulip bulb should feel solid, firm, and dense, with an intact papery outer tunic. Gently press the base plate and tip with your thumb. Any that give under your thumb, show mold, feel spongy, or have sunken yellow-brown patches should go in the trash.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Next, peel back a section of the papery tunic. Look carefully for sclerotia: tiny, hard, black or dark-brown resting bodies that resemble crushed pepper or poppy seeds. To help get a better look up close, the Jarlink 30X 60X Illuminated Jewelers Loupe, available from Amazon is equipped with bright LED illumination to check for those black sclerotia specks, as well as hidden scale lesions. These small sclerotia carry the tulip fire fungus between seasons. If you detect black specks or lesions, bag the bulb and throw it in the trash. Never toss diseased stock into home compost piles.

Resist the urge to plant your tulips while the ground is still warm. Botrytis tulipae fungal spores and resting sclerotia thrive in mild, damp soil conditions between 50°F and 65°F (10-18°C). Planting prematurely exposes bulbs to active soil-borne pathogens before the bulbs can establish robust roots. Delay your tulip planting until mid-to-late November or early December across most regions, after several hard overnight frosts have chilled the ground.

Soil temperatures should consistently measure below 50°F (10°C) at 6 inches (15cm). Cold soil suppresses fungal activity and forces dormant spores into inactivity. Planting after the first hard frosts is one of the most effective defenses against tulip fire. Even if an early frost hardens the surface, the soil beneath remains workable. Using a long-handled bulb planter like the Jardineer Bulb Transplanter from The Home Depot works well even in frost-encrusted fall soils.

Soil hygiene and thoughtful rotation are critical defenses against tulip fire. If your border suffered from tulip fire last spring, millions of sclerotia will have been shed into the earth as the leaves and flower petals decomposed. These resting bodies can survive in loam for 3-5 years, waiting to infect any new tulips that push up through the contaminated soil, and start the cycle all over again. Give that bed at least 3 years without tulips, and plant new bulbs somewhere that's never had the disease. Fill affected borders with non-host species that tulip fire cannot infect, such as daffodils (narcissus), alliums, grape hyacinths (muscari), or crocuses.

If bed space is tight, containers are an easy workaround. Transition your tulips into patio containers. However, always dump out old potting soil, sanitize containers with a dilute vinegar or mild bleach wash, and plant in fresh, sterile soilless potting mix enriched with perlite. A lovely blend is Espoma Organic Potting Mix, available from Walmart, which is free of garden pathogens, and gives a low-release nutrient boost.

A bulb that sits in soggy ground all winter is in trouble, whether tulip fire shows up or not. Good drainage is critical. Tulip bulbs thrive in moisture, but can rot quickly in stagnant water. Planting in heavy, compacted clay or low-lying depressions also creates damp conditions where fungal spores multiply rapidly. Check your planting site a day or so after a soaking rain. Water that is still standing there, or dirt that balls up and sticks to your boots, means the spot would drain too slowly for tulips.

Select a planting site situated on high ground or a gentle slope. If you garden on heavy clay, avoid digging individual narrow holes. Instead, excavate the whole planting area 8-10 inches (20-30cm) deep. Blend some horticultural grit or coarse sand into the soil to help with drainage. Alternatively, for persistently soggy gardens, skip the fight and grow your tulips in containers or raised beds. You can get small bags of best-selling Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot for just a few dollars, and sprinkle a few handfuls into the planting site (or use it in your containers!).

Crowded planting designs may look lush in magazine spreads, but tightly packed bulbs create stagnant, humid conditions. After a few years, offsets and daughter bulbs fill in a bit more each season, and after a while the leaves will crowd each other. If tulips are jammed together, leaves that touch will stay wet longer after rain or a heavy dew, and spores won't have far to go to get from one plant to the next.

Give your tulips room to breathe by spacing bulbs 4-6 inches (10-15cm) apart in all directions. Make sure the planting site is not jammed against a fence or the side of the house. Choose open, sunny sites with steady airflow. Use jute twine like Vivifying Natural Jute from Amazon looped around some wooden stakes to help mark your plantings. Also, if you are naturalizing tulips in mixed borders, lift and divide dense perennial clumps every few years before planting your bulbs.

Old tulip leaves don't just vanish when they're left on the soil. On plants that were sick, fresh sclerotia form on the dying tissue and drop into the bed, and they can stay there until tulips come up through that ground again. Infected leaves, decaying stem bases, and dropped flower petals all produce fresh sclerotia as they wither. Left untouched, it decomposes into the topsoil, recharging the fungal spore bank.

Before planting new bulbs, do a fall cleanup. Rake through your beds and clear out old leaves, spent stems, and decayed organic matter. Pull back mulch to inspect the soil, discarding any dried plant remnants and flower parts from the previous growing season. Make sure you bag these remnants instead of composting them. You can buy best-selling Fabulas Yard Waste Bags from Walmart in triple packs.

In spring, you need to stay proactive. Deadhead any spent flowers off suspect plants before their petals drop onto lower foliage, and clear out leaves and stems from anything that shows symptoms. Dig up any twisted firehead shoots, including the bulbs and adjacent soil. Do this the moment symptoms appear to keep airborne spores from spreading. Cleanup won't necessarily promise a clean bed, but it ensures there's a lot less fungus left behind to start the next round.

Once tulip fire takes hold in an established bed, it is one of the most persistent and frustrating bulb diseases to eradicate. So this fall care routine is massively beneficial in helping to break the fungal life cycle before it can cause damage. Take the right steps now when planting, and then you just have to wait for those first green shoots and a vibrant, spotless tulip display in spring.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. #7973. "Covert Contracts" Might Be Wrecking Your Relationship

If you’ve ever thought “after everything I do,” therapists say you might have one.

You did bedtime solo every single night this week. You did the baths, with all the splishing and the splashing and the bubble anarchy. You fielded the lightning round of existential questions at 8:47 p.m. (“Mommy, what happens to doggies when they die?”). You tucked everyone in and then did your regular closing-time routine to get the rest of the house buttoned up for bed.

So when Saturday morning rolls around, you’re planning to sleep in. You fully expect your partner to wake up and handle the kids, the breakfast, the early morning dog walking duties. The whole shebang. Tit for tat.

Then your kids are in your face before you can even pry your eyes open, wondering where their soccer cleats are or if you can get more juice. Cue the rage, right? OK, so here comes the uncomfortable gut-check… did you communicate your expectations to your partner? Or did you just sort of assume it was a done deal?

This scenario has been dubbed a "covert contract," and therapists say it can lead to a whole lot of resentment building up in a relationship over time. Here’s what experts want you to know about where this behavior comes from, how to spot it in your own actions, and how it differs from the imbalance of the invisible load.

“A covert contract is a deal only one person signed,” says Kristyn Carmichael, Esq., a family mediator, certified divorce financial analyst, and founder of Couples Solutions Center. “It sounds like ‘If I do X, you’ll do Y,’ but the other partner never saw the terms, never agreed to them, and usually doesn’t know the contract exists.”

And she often has a front-row seat to what happens when those deals go unaddressed for a prolonged period of time. “In mediation, I see the end stage of these: one spouse arrives with years of unpaid ‘invoices,’ and the other is honestly confused about what they owe.”

Cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety, trauma, and attachment therapist who authored The Somatic Healing Workbook, likens it to writing a big ol' agreement and assigning your partner an equally big role in it. Somehow, your partner is the only person unaware of said agreement.

But your partner being unaware doesn’t change the way you feel. The hurt is just as real as if they’d actually broken a promise. “In your brain, they did,” Groskopf explains.

Um, yes. One hundred percent. This was something every expert agreed on! However, the need itself isn’t the issue here; it’s the delivery method.

“The need underneath is reasonable, but if it’s not articulated overtly, then it’s unreasonable to think your partner would be a mind reader,” says Dr. Jenni Skyler, Adam & Eve’s resident sex and relationship therapist.

Already, as a busy working mom who happens to be the default parent, I instinctively start to feel myself bristle at this idea. No one tells me these things or what needs to be done — I just notice and do it because someone has to. The experts say that sort of thinking is a fast path to frustration.

“‘I want my partner to make an effort on my birthday’ is a totally reasonable desire,” Groskopf says. “‘I shouldn’t have to tell them what I want because if they really loved me, they’d already know’ is when it becomes problematic.”

Now, the experts were also abundantly clear that none of this means moms should just silently accept an unfair split.

“One person also shouldn’t have to become a household manager simply because they are more organized, quicker to notice what needs to be done, or less comfortable leaving things unfinished,” says Ilona Phillips, a psychotherapist and founder of Lotus Consulting in Ann Arbor, Michigan. “Expecting shared responsibility is reasonable. Expecting a partner to recognize an unspoken sacrifice and reciprocate exactly one-for-one can get partners in trouble.”

“If I ask for a break and you say no, that’s a direct rejection,” Carmichael says. “If I never ask, I’m protected from that, and I keep the moral high ground.” And, yes, there’s also that belief so many of us carry that “if I have to ask, it doesn’t count,” she adds, “as if a gesture only proves love when it’s unprompted.”

That belief tends to run deep, too (ask me how I know). Says Groskopf, “If you grew up learning that your needs were inconvenient, asking can feel incredibly vulnerable.” Instead of just asking, we end up creating these little litmus tests our partners don’t even know they’re taking.

She uses flowers as an example. If you ask for them, you know they showed up because you asked. But if your partner brings them on their own, "There’s this feeling that you were appreciated, that they noticed you, that you MATTER. And for someone who grew up feeling overlooked or emotionally neglected, that distinction can feel huge.”

Oof. The catch here is that this strategy often just backfires.

“There is a fear that if we directly communicate what we need, and that need is not met, we will be hurt,” explains Dr. Paulette Didia, a licensed clinical psychologist in New York City. “However, if we do not communicate what we need, our partner will not know, our partner will not do it, and we will be hurt anyway. We think hurting in our own mind ‘hurts less,’ and that is not true.”

Admittedly, the lines are a bit blurry. When you’re doing the lion’s share of invisible work in your home and family, it’s hard not to “keep score” or have a running tally in your head of what your partner did versus what you did.

Unfortunately, that scoreboard warps how both partners see each other.

“Once you develop a narrative that your partner isn’t doing enough, it becomes very easy to fill that bucket with examples of how they’re falling short. Meanwhile, your spouse feels like they’re always in the doghouse and starts to wonder if it’s even worth trying. One person is thinking, ‘Don’t you see how hard I’m working?’ while the other is thinking, ‘What did I do wrong now?’” says Mary McLaughlin, LCSW, a couples therapist and discernment counselor.

So while it’s fair to feel frustrated by an invisible (or visible) load imbalance, a little communication can go a long way. That’s true on both sides of the line. “Even if the score is unequal, if all parties know the score and acknowledge it and offer gratitude, this can offset resentment,” says Skyler.

Well, obviously this is tricky since you probably don’t know you’re making them. However, there are a few tells you can look for, according to the experts:

First and foremost, resist the urge to try settling years of “back pay.” You can’t Uno Reverse this one. Instead, focus on rewriting the terms and making sure you and your partner are, in fact, on the same page. Here are a few practical pointers from our pros on how to pull that off.

Didia asks couples to fill out a simple weekly worksheet together that includes tasks along with who does them and when. She has couples do this at the same time each week so that it doesn’t become one more thing Mom has to track, and they post the list where both can see it so no one becomes the default reminder.

If you want to follow suit, start by listing every task (big and small). Next, let each partner choose what they’ll take, and split the ones nobody wants. Very important info: The person who owns a task decides how and when it gets done. “Maybe you think this should be done by Monday, but your partner indicates it will be done by Wednesday,” Didia says. “Since it is their task, they get to decide and, by Tuesday, you will not already be annoyed.”

Phillips encourages a weekly check-in where partners take turns asking: What’s been working well between us? Is anything feeling off? Extra difficult? Frustrating as hell? Unacknowledged? And, finally, how can I be a better partner to you this week?

You may be tempted to stop doing certain things, like washing the dishes, hoping that someone will notice. That’s just a covert contract in a different outfit, says Phillips. And even if your partner does pick up the task, resentment can still linger. You might then think, Why did I have to stop before they noticed?

“Relationships change. What worked when you were first dating, before kids, 10 years ago may not work anymore,” reminds McLaughlin. “Couples need to renegotiate instead of assuming the old arrangement still works.”

When you realize you’re locked in a pattern that won’t budge, it’s probably time to see a couples therapist. Carmichael’s advice is to get help sooner rather than later. By the time couples land in her office, she says the covert contracts show up even in how they divorce, i.e., “I gave up my career, so I deserve more.”

At the end of the day, adds McLaughlin, “Resentment paired with avoidance is a particularly risky combination for couples.” And that means the fix, both annoyingly simple and incredibly hard, is saying what you need out loud… and holding each other accountable to those needs in a way that feels fair and equitable to you both.

#7972. Coach Mando's Advice For Dads Coaching Youth Sports

Brendan Wayne, the man who is The Mandalorian, has been coaching youth sports for more than 20 years. Here’s his advice to other coaches and parents on the sidelines.

When you watch the hit Star Wars TV show The Mandalorian — or the new film The Mandalorian and Grogu — and you start to wonder if there’s something about being a bounty hunter with a heart of gold that can help you with youth sports, you’re not nuts. It’s possible that just through osmosis, thanks to the motions of Mando himself, you’re getting some good sense of how to be a better sports parent. Here’s why: The actor who has played the body of The Mandalorian since 2019, Brendan Wayne, has been coaching soccer for 23 years. In addition to starting a new podcast, Hats & Helmets, Wayne is currently the coach of the Lady Lancers soccer team at Grant High School in California.

“I’ve played sports my whole life,” Wayne tells Fatherly. “It’s one of the greatest things a kid can learn to do.”

As the summer starts to give way to the beginning of school, we reached out to Wayne to get his core principles as a longtime coach of youth sports. This man may know how to calm down Baby Yoda, but that’s just acting. As a soccer coach, Wayne is an even bigger expert. Here’s his clear advice for parents of sporty kids, youth coaches, and why athletics can be great for all kinds of kids.

Wayne’s core coaching philosophy isn’t focused on winning; instead, he feels the only thing that makes a team is the notion of togetherness.

Many parents have been there. The game is going a certain way, and you can’t help yourself with your thoughts. You’ve shouted out something; you’ve even has words with a ref or the coach. What should you do? Wayne’s feelings are very, very clear.

Even as a coach, Wayne doesn’t shout at his players while the game is actually happening. The coaching comes before the game happens, not from the sidelines.

Sometimes, a kid can lose interest in their sport. Or maybe they’re feeling like they’re not part of the team. What can coaches and sports parents do? For Wayne, it’s not about quitting right away but about looking at athletics more holistically.

As an actor and performer, Wayne knows a thing or two about how to keep all aspects of his body in shape — fitting into that Mandalorian armor doesn’t just happen by accident. One of his biggest beliefs, which he applies to youth sports, is that a person has to look at the big picture. For Wayne, it’s all about making sure kids are getting different kinds of exercises.

If you do need to say something to a kid who looks frustrated out there in the game, keep in mind that most of these kids aren’t going pro. Some might, but that’s not the point of this moment.

When Wayne sees one of his kids on the field and they need inspiration, he sometimes just tries to lighten the moment.

#7971. Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage

Home / Getting Pregnant / Miscarriage & Loss

When I lost my baby, I knew it was a day I’d never forget. And then I did.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Content warning: Discussion of pregnancy loss ahead.

I was cleaning my kitchen, pop music blaring from a speaker, when I glanced at the digital calendar on my counter. That’s when I saw it—the butterfly emoji that flutters every August 21 to memorialize the day I lost my pregnancy.

I was gutted. But this time it wasn’t because of the miscarriage. It was because I forgot. For the first time in 10 years, the date my baby’s heart stopped beating had slipped my mind.

It’s not hard for me to bring myself back to that day. At my 12-week appointment, the doctor ran a fetal doppler across my belly, searching for a heartbeat she would never find. I watched the crease between her eyebrows deepen as she moved the wand around. She tried to reassure me there could be a reason she couldn’t find the heartbeat. Still, it made sense to get an ultrasound.

I headed off to a new location. I didn’t call anyone, doing my best to will “it’s fine” into existence. I sat nervously in the waiting room, tapping my leg up and down as I listened for my name.

When it was my turn, I laid back on the table, prepped for the squeeze of cool jelly on my stomach, then watched a screen on the wall as the ultrasound tech poked around to find my baby.

And there it was. The makings of my second born lit up on the screen. Those images are always a bit tough to discern, but I could clearly see a head, a body, and four limbs. But those limbs weren’t moving, and the tech stayed quiet. She pressed buttons, took snapshots, and kept her gaze trained squarely on her computer screen. When she finished, she said, “The doctor will be in to talk to you,” then scurried out the door.

Seconds later someone else popped in and asked me to follow them to another room. I now realize I was taking up precious space near the ultrasound equipment. They’d need it for their next appointment, and the news I was about to hear might stun me in place for some time.

The moment is crystal clear in my memory even ten years later. I remember the hard plastic chair I sat in. I remember looking around the room and realizing that half of it was used for storage. There were boxes of papers and remnants of mailers alongside random supplies waiting for their real homes. Next to me, a box of tissues sat on a small table.

When the doctor walked in, he introduced himself. I don’t remember his name, but I’ll never forget his somber look when he said, “It’s not good news.” The floor falling out from beneath me. I called my husband in tears, barely able to say, “There’s no heartbeat,” then made a desperate call to my mom to share the same news.

I don’t remember how I got back to my grandmother’s house, where she was watching my 2-year-old son. I know I drove there, but the memory is hazy, overlaid with the sadness, terror and anxiety that were coursing through me.

When I arrived, I collapsed into my grandmother’s arms. “They couldn’t find a heartbeat,” I said, fighting back tears as my son watched us intently. She tightened her grip on me and let me dissolve.

I suffered a missed miscarriage—my body didn’t recognize that the baby growing inside had died. But based on its size and development, doctors were able to tell me that the heart likely stopped beating at 10.5 weeks. That’s how I came to mark August 21 as the day my baby died.

In the years that followed, I anxiously awaited both that date and my due date as they crept closer. I knew they would be hard. Over the first couple of years, I’d plan for unproductive days, knowing I’d fall back into my grief. I’d spend the morning each August 21 remembering the day I found out, going over every detail as I let the tears rain down. I’d search for signs of butterflies, which became a hopeful symbol to me in the wake of my miscarriage.

But ten years later, I was caught up in the details of a very busy life. I’m a working mom with two school-aged kids who spends much of my time chauffeuring them between playdates and sports practices.

It’s likely a good sign that August 21 no longer looms over me like a dark cloud. In those early years of letting the grief wash over me in full force, I gave my mind, body and heart the space to release its tension and ache. But forgetting the date brought its own type of grief. It was a reminder of how far I’ve come, and how far my baby never did.

Ten years later, I still grieve my miscarriage, but that grief has evolved. I will always wonder what that little life would have become, and why they weren’t given the chance. I will always take a moment to pause and remember the hope, joy and love I felt in the early weeks of that pregnancy, even if I need the calendar to remind me to do so.

And most importantly, I will always talk about it. With time, grief has lessened its stranglehold on my heart and emotions. What remains of my grief is more like a tool. It appears when I need to be a supporter. It boosts my voice so I can help others in the throes of their own despair.

One in 4 women will experience pregnancy or infant loss in their lifetime. I’m a 1-in-4, and I hope sharing my story helps someone else feel less alone in their pain, no matter where she is on her grieving journey.

October is Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month. If you or someone you know is struggling with a postpartum mental health challenge after a pregnancy or infant loss, call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline at 1-833-9-HELP4MOMS (1-800-943-5746). This free, confidential service provides access to trained counselors and resources 24 hours a day, 7 days a week in English, Spanish, and more than 60 other languages. They can offer support and information related to before, during, and after pregnancy.

#7970. The Butler Didn't Do It

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Todd Butler's bare Senate Judiciary Committee Questionnaire.

Todd Butler has now posted his questionnaire for the Senate Judiciary Committee. Here is the chronology Butler offers for his nomination:

On June 29, 2026, Senator Roger Wicker contacted me about a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. I spoke with Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith the following day. On July 1, 2026, an official from the White House Counsel's Office contacted me to arrange an interview. On July 13, 2026, I interviewed with officials from the White House Counsel's Office. Following my interview, I received periodic updates from Senator Wicker about the process. On October I, 2026, President Trump called to inform me that he planned to nominate me for a position on the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

There is a very relevant date missing here. On September 28, 2026, Judge Southwick publicly announced that he would take senior status. Yet three months earlier, Senator Wicker contacted Butler about the potential vacancy.

As I said from the outset, the fix was in. There was some sort of deal involving Wicker, Southwick, and the White House. I'm sure this interview was pro forma. and doubt any other candidates were interviewed. Judge Southwick could have announced his intentions at any time in August or early September, but he waited until the last possible moment to jam up the process, and ensure Butler would not go down. I do hope at least one Senator asks Butler if he is aware of any communications in which Judge Southwick, directly or indirectly, conditioned his willingness to take senior status if Butler is the nominee.

As for the rest of the SJQ, let's just say Butler's pantry is bare. Or, the Butler didn't do it.

Butler went to law school between 2005 and 2008, but he wasn't a member of the Federalist Society. That makes sense, as he wrote critically of Justice Scalia, originalism, and the Second Amendment. He wasn't a member while he clerked. Indeed, he didn't become a member of the Federalist Society until 2016. I suspect lots of people joined before or after Trump's victory. It would help with career prospects. He has never held any leadership positions in FedSoc. But rest assured that he was active in the Inn of Court and the Mississippi Bar, holding several leadership positions.

Butler has extensive experience in employment law. In addition to the publications I flagged, Butler speaks and writes often about the EEOC, FLSA, and related topics of municipal law. His only professional exposure to constitutional law involves defendant local officials who are sued for violating First Amendment rights. After Olivier v. City of Brandon, his most significant case was as defense counsel in a wrongful death case. He taught at the Mississippi College of Law "periodic[ally]" between 2008 and 2016 but does not recall which semesters he taught. He also does not have copies of the syllabi.

Here is how Butler describes his pro bono work:

Over the course of my career, I have accepted pro bono clients, typically through the Mission First Legal Aid Clinic or the Mississippi Volunteers Lawyers Project. I have assisted with adoptions, child visitation matters, and other domestic issues. I also have provided pro bono services to a local church, including contract review and procedure drafting, in connection with the operation of a faith-based children's center. I advised a local pastor on a land acquisition that he is considering using for a fellowship facility. And I have volunteered, along with others at my law firm, at Stewpot Community Services, where we served meals to people experiencing homelessness.

There is no pro bono work that would remotely be associated with the conservative legal movement. And no, working for a church does not necessarily make a person conservative.

If I were to show you this questionnaire, without any knowledge of Mississippi politics, would you possibly think this was a viable record for the Fifth Circuit? No.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7969. 10 Foreign True Crime Documentaries To Scratch Two Itches At Once

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? Why not do both?

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? It’s the universal conundrum. On the one hand, the world is a big and beautiful place full of opportunities to eat delicious food and meet new people and wear hats you would never wear at home. On the other hand, there are true crime stories that need to be solved by you in your pajamas on the couch under a weighted blanket.

How do you scratch both of those itches? Well, you could travel the world seeking out true crimes to solve yourself, but that would get pricey and probably pretty dangerous. You don’t want to become the subject of your own true crime documentary, after all. Instead, settle in on a long, rainy weekend (or when it’s bright and sunny, I’m not judging) to watch these engrossing true crime documentaries set in beautiful locations around the world. It’s safer and the snacks are cheaper.

In 1996, French film producer Sophie Toscan du Plantier was found murdered outside her remote holiday cottage in the small village of Toormore. West Cork two days before Christmas. Sophie was just 39 years old and mom to son Pierre-Louis. A local journalist was one of the first to report her murder, and quickly became the main suspect. Netflix’s three-part docuseries Sophie - A Murder in West Cork covers not only Sophie’s tragic death, but also the struggle between Ireland and France to convict the killer.

Amy Lynn Bradley was just 23 years old when she went missing from the Royal Caribbean cruise ship Rhapsody of the Sea one early morning in March 1998. The ship was en route to the island of Curaçao. Her room showed no sign of a struggle, and several items were left behind. Authorities initially considered Bradley’s disappearance to be a potential accident or suicide, but Netflix’s 2025 three-part docuseries Amy Bradley is Missing speculates on several other possibilities that could have happened in the sunny tropics.

We do not love a scam artist. Especially one who preys on women looking for love, as Israeli conman Shimon Hayut aka Simon Leviev did between 2017 to 2019. Hayut swindled millions of dollars from women in the Netherlands, Norway, and other countries around Europe, leaving them destitute and broken-hearted. That’s the bad news. The good news is the way these women eventually found each other, banding together to bring Hayut to justice and try to reclaim their money. Netflix’s 2022 documentary The Tinder Swindler tells the story of three women who lost nearly everything to Hayut, and how they came together to bring him down.

The Netflix 2026 three-part docuseries Should I Marry a Murderer? will stay with you for a long time after the fact. Not just because it’s set in the gorgeous Scottish countryside, but because of the perspective it offers on what it might actually look like to find out the man you love is genuinely a murderer. Caroline Muirhead met handsome Scottish farmer Alexander “Sandy” McKellar on Tinder, and the two got engaged in 2020 after a whirlwind four month romance. When McKellar confessed to a murder that happened three years earlier, Muirhead stays with him. Told from her modern day perspective, Should I Marry a Murderer? Is an unflinching glimpse at what we might be willing to overlook in the name of love.

Vittorio Emanuele was nine years old when his family was exiled from Italy in 1946. His father was King Umberto II, and Vittorio was meant to be a prince until Italy voted to create a republic without the royal family. Living a life of luxurious exile, Vittorio was on the French island of Corsica in 1978 when he was involved in the death of 19-year-old German tourist Dirk Hamer. Netflix’s 2023 three-part series The King Who Never Was features interviews with Vittorio himself, as well as Dirk Hamer’s family members who were determined to see the privileged deposed royal charged with Dirk’s murder.

Michel Fourniret confessed to killing 11 women and one man in the picturesque Ardennes region of France between 1987 to 2003, making him one of the most notorious serial killers in modern French history. The Belgian killer only confessed after his seemingly submissive wife, Monique Olivier, provided police with enough information to force his hand. Which meant, of course, that she knew something of her husband’s crimes. More than police might have suspected, if the 2023 Netflix limited series Monique Olivier: Accessory to Evil proves anything. Olivier might have even been a willing participant in her husband’s horrific crimes. Chilling.

Fair warning for the 2019 five-part Netflix docuseries Who Killed Little Gregory? - the entire series revolves around the awful kidnapping and murder of 4-year-old Grégory Villemin in a small village in eastern France. Grégory’s murder has never been solved, and this docuseries delves into the disturbing allegations that members of his own extended family might have murdered the little boy. This one is equal parts difficult to watch and completely engrossing.

If you’re looking for some real-life Scandinavian noir to get you through the dark nights of fall, you’ll want to check out The Lørenskog Disappearance, Netflix’s five-part docuseries based on the true story of real life Norwegian billionaire Tom Hagan. Hagan’s wife Anne-Elisabeth Hagan went missing from the couple’s opulent home in October 2018, and a ransom note asking for nine million euros was left in her wake. The police originally believed Anne-Elisabeth was kidnapped, but began to suspect murder when the alleged kidnappers didn’t continue to reach out. While this 2022 limited series is a drama and not a straight documentary, it really delivers on Scandi vibes and billionaire intrigue.

British tourist Grace Millane was taking a gap year to travel the world when she ended up in New Zealand in 2018. She planned to head back home to her family for Christmas. She never made it back home. Millane was reported missing by her family, with police conducting a massive search in Auckland and the surrounding area before zeroing in on Jesse Kempson, her final Tinder date. The 2024 documentary The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane on Amazon Prime, features interview tapes with Kempson as he is interrogated by police, and his subsequent attempt to use the so-called “rough sex murder” defense for killing the 22-year-old. On her birthday.

If you’ve been thinking of spending a bit of time in the UK along the coast, the Apple TV series Coastal Killers will either intrigue you or scare you off, depending on your perspective. Instead of focusing on just one true crime story, Coastal Killers has eight seasons of stories of mayhem in lovely little seaside towns in the UK...

...Which should keep you busy as you plan your next potential trip.

Why plant an invasive ornamental tree when you could have one that's just as beautiful but brings so much more to the garden?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Look, I'm calling it: the Bradford pear has had its moment. For years, its blooms have been everywhere, but now its the turn of an even prettier native tree to take its spot – and it definitely helps that it's a triple threat when it comes to blossoms, berries, and beautiful fall foliage!

I know, I know; it's a big claim, especially as so many people rate the Bradford pear for its frothy white flowers, not to mention the pretty show its leaves put on when fall arrives. Still, there's a less attractive side to Bradford pears – and I'm not just talking about the unpleasant stench its flowers put out.

That's right, folks! As well as being notoriously unpleasant-smelling, the Bradford pear's branches are prone to splitting, and these trees can contribute to the spread of invasive Callery pears, too. So, if you're thinking about planting a new ornamental tree, it might be time to consider a more wildlife-friendly alternative.

My suggested swap for the invasive Bradford pear? Why, the serviceberry, of course!

This beautiful native tree pretty much does it all; think plenty of springtime charm in the form of beautiful blossoms, followed by delicious berries, and wrapped up nicely with some gorgeous fall foliage. And unlike Bradford pear, it's a valuable addition to a garden that welcomes local wildlife.

Serviceberry, also known as juneberry or shadbush, belongs to the Amelanchier genus. Depending on the species and variety, it can grow as a large shrub or a small tree, making it a useful option for gardens where a full-sized shade tree would be too much.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It is one of those plants that gives back much more than it takes, providing an early source of nectar and pollen for pollinators, sweet edible berries that work brilliantly in pies, jams and other homemade treats (although birds love them, too), and gorgeous fall foliage that promises to paint your yard in shades of yellow, orange and red before winter arrives.

All that from one relatively compact native tree? You'd better believe it!

One of the things I love most about serviceberry (as if all of the above weren't reason enough to be a fan!) is that most species grow well in full sun or partial shade, making it more accessible to people with all sorts of gardens. Just be sure to pop it in a spot with well-draining soil, as they won't appreciate sitting in waterlogged ground.

For many homeowners, this native tree is a no-brainer, because what do you mean it offers the spring flowers that made Bradford pear so popular, along with edible fruit, beautiful fall color and valuable food for wildlife? Tick, tick, tick, and tick!

While it won't necessarily grow as quickly or have the same uniform, upright shape as a Bradford pear, I think that's part of its appeal. And, with the world changing as quickly as it is, I think we can all agree that a garden tree should do more than look pretty for a few weeks each year.

A native beauty that gives back to local critters and puts out fruit that taste every bit as good as blueberries, then? Sign me up!

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

#7966. The Awkward Truth About Gym Class

Pretend you’re a tree. This was my earliest memory of physical education: our teacher, a tall and thin woman whose broad nimbus of dark hair was edged with gray, asking us to make-believe. By, as I understood it, not moving. In gym class. I was in second grade, and I was already confused. Somewhere here in my elementary school’s wood-floored gymnasium, I knew, there were ropes to climb, mats to tumble on, balls to kick and throw and dodge. And yet we were being corralled into this dumbed-down modern dance — the kind of hippie sh*t, I would later understand, that was typical of our Western Massachusetts college town.

Not that I was craving, or ever did crave, a traditional gym class. I was not made for gym. I was small — perpetually the second shortest boy in my grade — and slight and uninterested in the big sports that make up the bulk of public-school gym. I did not own a catcher’s mitt; no sane, responsible adult would let this shrimp play football.

At the same time, I was physical. I was a kid, after all. I wanted to run around, try a handstand, lift a dumbbell, shoot a basket, make a goal. And as uncoordinated and unenthusiastic as I was, I was not entirely untalented. I remember running a seven-minute mile in fourth grade. I could touch my toes and put one foot behind my head. My friend Jason and I competed to see who would be the first to knock out 60 sit-ups in a minute. I don’t remember who won.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class.

Those achievements and activities, however, had nothing to do with gym class as I experienced it. In the same way that English class was not designed to make philistines love literature, or biology to inspire dedication to the scientific method, gym class was not about converting us into athletes. Instead, it was a class for the kids who already were athletes, who played baseball and field hockey for fun, who owned weight machines at home, who didn’t need to sit through the gym teacher’s confounding explanation of what it meant to be “offsides.” I didn’t begrudge them their special class. I could spell and do algebra. They could throw an arcing spiral. This was the way of the world, even in a Massachusetts town full of ex-hippies.

And that all would have been just fine — if gym class had stuck with the most mainstream of sports. I could suck at soccer and blow at basketball, because who cared? Instead, gym class branched out, and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Swimming was a particular source of trauma. When I was 8, during a year my family spent living in Brighton, England, I was so tearfully reluctant to get in the pool that the headmaster of the school had to personally throw me in. And as I got older, the trauma morphed: Back in Massachusetts, the locker room after eighth-grade swimming lessons was a horror movie — I, the underdeveloped shrimp, had to undress surrounded by my Sasquatchian contemporaries. I have a memory of once changing entirely inside a locker, but that can’t be real. Those things were barely 10 inches wide. But another memory is definitely real: During one class, I dived into the deep end — and the force of the water as I entered yanked my swimsuit to my ankles. I don’t know how I had the wherewithal to pull them up before surfacing, but I did. I guess I was learning something.

The psychosexual torture continued when gym class turned, for one whole day, to ballroom dance class. Already awkward around girls, not to mention the implied romance of ballroom dance, I had the misfortune to be paired with Turtle Butt. Who was Turtle Butt? I don’t know. She was a girl I’d never spoken to, but one of my good friends had decided to call her Turtle Butt, even though, as far as I could tell, her butt did not resemble a turtle. And I was going to have to dance with her! Oh, the humiliation!

Gym class has always branched out from mainstream sports — and in those more marginal activities, it became an hour of dread.

Nearly 40 years later, I can now acknowledge that the humiliation was solely in my own head. I remember the potential embarrassment with infinitely more clarity than I remember any actual jeers or taunts, because there were none. But such is the world of the adolescent, where fears and anxieties dwarf reality.

And what I feared most of all was being seen. In other classes this didn’t happen. You might know where the Mason-Dixon Line was — or not. You might know how to deploy the quadratic formula — or not. Either way, you were not exposing anything about yourself other than your intellectual ability, or lack thereof.

It was similar in gym class. We all knew that some kids had it and some didn’t, and there was no shame in being terrible. (Asthma reduced my mile time to 20 minutes by eighth grade. But so what?) The difference, however, was that in gym class, unlike in history or math, you were a physical being. Strip away your ability to perform, and there you still stood, surrounded by your classmates, in sneakers and sweats or the jeans and T-shirt you wore to school that morning. You could pretend you’re a tree all you want — you remained visible: your prepubescent stature, your hairless lack of muscle tone, your terrapin posterior. There were no desks to hide behind, no escape from their eyes and their judgment.

No escape — except, perhaps, to grow up a little. In high school, my family moved to Southeastern Virginia, a place you’d think would have a sports and gym-class culture more extreme than that of the academic Yankees. Instead, gym was even more of an afterthought, not even required after sophomore or maybe junior year. Just like in second grade, I was confused. The school was full of jocks — guys who played soccer and football, girls on the field hockey team — and yet gym class was lackadaisical at best. Driver’s ed occupied a couple of months of the curriculum, and on Fridays, we’d ride a school bus to a nearby bowling alley, where nerds like me, who had no hope of throwing a strike, could at least show off by knowing how to score the game correctly.

Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not.

In fact, I considered the bowling alley my place — because I was there all the time, after school. Technically, not in the bowling alley, but just outside, where almost every day I would meet my skateboarder friends to ride the concrete drainage ditch next to its parking lot. In high school, skating had become my life, my all-consuming hobby, my… my… sport? Yes, my sport! After having failed at all of the mainstream sports, I’d finally found this one sweaty, filthy, wonderful way to be an athlete (though I would never have used that word back then). And while I wasn’t pro material, I wasn’t too bad at it, either. I could hold my own among my friends, at competitions in Virginia Beach, on road trips to Richmond and Washington, D.C. And more important, I could do so without fretting about being seen, in some unspeakable way, by the kids around me. Skateboarding required us to accept one another, in all our foibles and weirdnesses. Because if we didn’t, then who would we skate with?

I stuck with skateboarding for most of a decade, before aging out postcollege and taking up distance running and, more recently, rock climbing. As with skateboarding, I’m pretty good at both, if not truly exceptional, and I appreciate the physical experience of each in ways I could not have imagined in high school. At times, I’ve wondered: If gym class had taught us how to run, or how to scale a boulder, would I have discovered and loved those sports decades earlier? Somehow, I doubt it. Like so much of school, gym class had little to do with real life beyond offering up a few superficial options that might, one day, many years later, be of interest. Or not. What mattered was what happened after school, in every sense of the term. Still, gym class did teach me this one important lesson about public education: If you make like a tree, you can leave.

#7965. 6 ways to make homework less of a battle when your kid has ADHD

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A child psychiatrist on getting through the after-school hours without a standoff.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 28, 2026

Tonight’s homework is a single worksheet. It’s been 50 minutes. Your kid has sharpened every pencil in the house, visited the bathroom twice, and is now face-down on the floor insisting it’s impossible. You can feel your patience slipping by the second.

If homework battles turn your evenings into a standoff, you’re far from alone, especially if your child has ADHD. About 1 in 9 US kids have been diagnosed with the condition , and the American Academy of Pediatrics says it can profoundly affect a child’s academic achievement. For families managing ADHD, the after-school stretch is often the hardest part of the day.

There’s a reason those hours are so trying. By the time a child with ADHD gets home,  they’ve spent “six or seven hours working harder than their classmates to sit still and focus,” says Michael Morse, MD, a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist who directs the ADHD & Anxiety Center at Alvord Baker and is an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University. That effort is used up, and for many kids the medication has worn off too, so “the after-school brain is often a tired brain.”

The resistance usually isn’t a matter of defiance. Executive function, the set of skills needed for getting started, planning and keeping track of steps, develops more slowly in kids with ADHD. That’s why a child can freeze in front of an assignment they’re fully capable of completing, and why the thing that helps is making the first step smaller rather than pushing harder.

The worst time to start homework is the moment your child walks through the door. The school day has already drained the same systems homework demands, so Morse suggests framing the immediate after-school window as a time to refuel. “A snack with some protein comes first, because after-school hunger makes both focus and mood worse,” he says. Movement comes next, whether that’s riding a bike or walking the dog, which burns off the day’s tension and helps many kids with ADHD settle. Make the break predictable with a clear end, and pick a consistent homework time that comes after the break and well before your child is too fried to think.

Most importantly, hold off on screens. “The transition from screens to homework can be particularly painful,” Morse says, so it’s usually easier not to turn them on after school at all.

“A task feels too big when a child can’t see where it starts,” Morse says. Many kids with ADHD freeze in front of a big assignment because their brain can’t break it into steps on its own, so the task is to shrink the first step until it feels easy.

Say a book report is due in two weeks. Sit down together and have your child break it into pieces: choose the book, read one chapter, jot notes on the main character. Then put each piece on a calendar so the deadline isn’t, in Morse’s words, “a cliff at the end.” For a single night’s work, 10 math problems can become two sets of five with a break in between. And when your child finishes a piece, say so out loud, since that small win makes the next one easier to start. (Younger kids need the pieces smaller and the check-ins more frequent.)

“Players usually appreciate coaches who run laps with them,” Morse says. He encourages parents to be “a coach and a model, not an enforcer.” In practice that can look like sitting at the kitchen table with your own work, while your child does theirs. A calm adult nearby helps many kids with ADHD get started and keep going. What a coach doesn’t do is finish the work so it comes back perfect, “because then the teacher never sees what the child can really do,” Morse says. The job is to help plan the night and praise the effort while leaving the outcome up to your child.

When homework turns into a power struggle, handing a little control back to your child can often defuse it. Offer two options you’re happy with either way, like “Math or reading first?” or “Before dinner or after, but before screens.” “A choice gives a child some control,” Morse says, which can take the fight out of the room before it starts. (If homework is still a daily battle no matter what you try, Morse notes a tutor can often take the coaching role with less friction than a parent.)

Some nights, the right move is to stop. “A parent should call it when the homework is no longer teaching anything or when substantial conflict emerges,” Morse says. If your child is in tears, exhausted or stuck on the same problem despite your help, more pushing won’t produce learning. “It mostly produces a worse night and a child who dreads the next one,” he says. When you stop, have your child’s back by sending the teacher a short note about how long they worked and where they got stuck. Most teachers would rather know.

“Your relationship with your child is more important than any assignment,” Morse says, and that relationship is what carries a kid through years of school. Kids with ADHD already hear a lot of criticism, and “if homework turns every evening into a battle, home stops feeling like the place where they’re accepted.”

Some homework problems are too big to solve at the kitchen table. “I’d start advocating when the problem looks bigger than effort,” Morse says. Watch for homework that routinely takes far longer than the teacher intended, work your child understands but can’t get written down or turned in, or nights that keep ending in tears. Those point to a gap between what the assignment asks and what your child can do right now, and pushing harder at home won’t close it.

Start by telling the teacher how long the work is actually taking. Some kids need more formal support through a 504 plan or an individualized education program, the school plans that put accommodations in writing. This matters especially for girls, Morse says, “whose late-night effort can keep their grades up and hide how much they’re struggling.”

As kids get older, Morse’s advice is to hand over the wheel gradually, with middle school as the moment to watch, when additional teachers and long-term projects arrive just as parents tend to step back. Teach your child to use a planner, check in briefly each evening, and let them take on more as they show they can. The long-term goal is teaching a kid which tasks will always need a system or a helper, because “knowing when to ask for help is one of the most valuable skills a teenager can carry into adult life.”

That need goes well beyond ADHD. Accountability partners and body doubles, “people whose quiet company helps you start and stay on task,” work for nearly everyone. “Not everyone knows to ask,” Morse says.

Peonies are pretty, we know, but peony-like tulips give you way more petals for far less effort, and you can plant the spring-flowering bulbs in November.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We all adore the richly-colored, ruffled petals of peonies but if you’ve only got one plant in your garden, the show’s over in little more than a week. Plant some peony-like tulip bulbs, however, and you can enjoy months of very similar-looking flowers from early April all through May and sometimes even into June. These double tulips couldn’t be easier to grow, and this month is the exact right time to plant the bulbs.

Most tulips have six petals but a natural genetic hiccup capitalized upon by plant breeders means that some cultivars can have up to 50 packed into a single bloom. They’re known as double tulips, and their petal-explosion flowers look remarkably similar to peony blooms. Typically hardy in zones 3-8, they’re some of the best tulip varieties to kickstart spring in your garden, and the most striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November.

The trick to enjoying months of flowers is to pick a pair of tulip varieties, one that opens early and one that blooms a little later. Early-flowering double tulips (officially known as peony-like tulips) begin blooming early in April. These tend to have shorter, sturdy 12-16 inch-high stems so stand up well to spring storms. Their tight layers of petals protect the flower core from cold weather, too, so each bloom can last for around 3 weeks – far longer than a standard tulip.

Late-flowering double tulips (known as peony-flowered tulips) bloom late April through May and are even more spectacular with huge flower heads on taller 16-24 inch-high stems. Because they're so top-heavy, these are more vulnerable to toppling in strong winds so in an exposed garden, give them a sheltered spot.

So, if you love peony flowers and you're wondering what to plant in November, look no further. Part of the Weekend Wins series, planting double tulips that look like peonies is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward.

When shopping for double tulips, it's important that bulbs are big enough to fuel all those petals so early in the year, so always buy from a quality supplier. All our recommendations are for 10 bulbs.

‘Lorenzo’ gets spring off to a cheery start with long-lasting blooms in a luminous apricot-orange softly edged in creamy yellow, all through April.

With enormous blooms opening in late April and peaking through May, ‘Gudoshnik Double' has painterly petals streaked in yellow, orange and red.

A few double tulips are fragranced, and 'Avant Garde’ opens its buds in early April to release a sweet, floral perfume with beautifully fresh undertones.

In late April, ‘Pistache’ brings more creamy-white petals, this time splashed with wine red, and a wonderful scent of almonds and pistachios into May.

‘Foxy Foxtrot’ wakes up early in April, opening a lovely lemon yellow then gaining rich, warm tones of apricot, salmon-pink and honeyed gold.

In mid-to-late April, ‘Amazing Grace’ starts in a soft lavender pink with green accents, then shade-shifts into a deep rose tone that lasts deep into May.

In early April, ‘Royal Acres’ blooms open into bowls of intensely-colored, velvety magenta petals, often with a silvery sheen along the ruffled edges.

‘Dream Touch’ takes over the show from late April through May with enormous purple blooms, their striking petals prettily edged in white.

Though officially classified as a late tulip, ‘Mariage’ blooms in mid-April with deeply ruffled flowers in the prettiest pale rose-pink, and lasts into May.

‘Wild Romance’ adds creamy white petals with blushing pink picotee edges from late April through May, opening to reveal dramatic jet-black stamens.

‘Marshmallow’ opens in early April with a splash of bi-colored raspberry pink and ivory white petals, with a few green streaks for good measure.

Keeping the drama going, ‘Black Hero’, blooms from late April through May with ruffles of velvety deep-maroon petals that have a super sheen.

Growing spectacular double tulip flowers from fall-planted bulbs couldn’t be easier, and November is the exact right time to get them in the ground.

#7963. How To Initiate Sex Again After A Long Drought, Because We've All Been There

It’s all about easing in (and examining what got you here.)

Work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy. It’s enough to have you laid out on the couch, carcass style, at the end of a regular day. When something actually goes wrong, like the kids get sick or a work project keeps you at your desk late, it’s even harder to imagine getting it up at the end of the day. No matter how much you love your spouse, sex droughts come for everyone at some point (ahem, many points) throughout a relationship. If it’s been a while and you want to get back in the game, here’s how to reinitiate.

Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again. It almost feels like you have to acknowledge the drought, and therefore the bad things that led up to it, or perhaps the parts you’ve both played in letting it drag on. It’s just a lot, but try not to blame yourself.

“Sex droughts are far more common than pop culture would have us believe. They're certainly nothing to be ashamed of, nor do they represent a ‘failure,’” says Angie Rowntree, ABS, board-certified sexologist and founder and filmmaker behind the award-winning ethical adult film site Sssh.com. “Life happens. Bodies get sick or injured, or may have different needs. Children are born and demand your time and care. Older parents may need care. Jobs might change. Any number of stresses and interruptions in your life can upend what was your regularly scheduled Saturday date night or sap you of the carefree mojo you’d usually bring to the bedroom. None of that is a shortcoming, or is anyone’s fault.”

Every couple is different in terms of how much sex is enough for them to feel happy with it, so remember that you don’t have to meet some made-up quota of intimate evenings per week. If you are ready to get back into the groove, though, here’s how to start.

First, initiating sex after a long break comes with natural stress and pressure. If it doesn’t land with your spouse, don’t let it get you down.

“Sometimes we need a little warm-up before we get back in the saddle, so to speak. Start small. Don’t hint with memes, but act. Physical touch and flirtation are things that ignite foreplay in the mind. Kiss for a little longer than usual before you leave. Send a suggestive text during the day. Get into bed and cuddle, but without immediately reaching below the belt. You’re essentially reminding each other that you still desire each other,” Rowntree says.

It’s also totally OK to address the elephant in the room, Rowntree says. Tell your partner, “I miss being close to you. Can we make some time tonight?” This way you’re giving them an invitation and creating a little anticipation all at once.

If you go for it and your partner turns you down, don’t turn a situational no into a personal one, says Rowntree.

“When they say, ‘Honey, I’m tired,’ it becomes, ‘You don’t turn me on anymore.’ The longer you’ve been together, the more history there can be attached to that moment. If one person is usually initiating sex, or usually declining it, those long-term behavior patterns can make a huge impact.”

If there’s longstanding angst in your relationship around who initiates and how often, that in and of itself can lead to more sex droughts. It’s something to have a “frank discussion” about, Rowntree advises. During that conversation, you want to figure out how to separate “I don’t want sex right now” from “I don’t want you.”

“You want to frame your communication in a way that maintains your partner’s desirability and your interest. For instance: ‘I’m exhausted tonight, but can we cuddle?’ or, ‘Why don’t I wake you up and we can take a shower together tomorrow morning before I have to go?’ The point is, you’re declining the timing, not rejecting your partner, or giving them any ambiguity about your attraction to them.”

“Sometimes it really is the little things that turn a ‘meh, maybe’ into a spark that goes all the way. Also, please stop feeling like you need elaborate Instagram-worthy seduction schemes. There’s no reason to overcomplicate basic human desire. Put on music and pour a drink together after work. Send a flirty text before you get home. Give them a lingering kiss in the kitchen that morning. Or just say, ‘Why don’t we go to bed early tonight? I’ve missed you.’”

#7962. 10 Great Sports Docs & True-Life Stories To Stream With Your Kids Right Now

From inspiring stories to crucial moments in history to cutting edge contermporary atheletes, there’s a great co-viewing experience for everyone.

Finding movies and TV that please everyone can be tough. But if you’ve got a sporty kid, screen time is a great opportunity. Sure, there’s old-school sports movie like The Sandlot or A League of Their Own — complete with inspirational messages and strong moral codes. But why go for fictional sports stories when you can get the real thing?

Sports docuseries, or true-to-life dramatized sports stories, are great to watch with young athletes. They tell inspirational tales and maybe even give them a real-life role model in the meantime. From a variety of different sports to a selection of different formats, we’ve thought about the watchability and the relevance of each of these selections. There should be something for everyone in this list. And, at the very least, with each, you and your kid will learn something.

This documentary film focuses on several different Paralympic athletes, all of whom have truly amazing stories. Warning for parents: This documentary is not for the faint of heart, as some of the physical challenges are truly harrowing. For example, Bebe Vio — who inspired the name of the documentary — lost all of her limbs to meningitis at the age of 11. She nonetheless went on to become a wheelchair fencer. Deeply inspiring, this doc is great for teens interested in sports and perhaps great for all of us to have a little perspective on the amazing nature of the human spirit.

The 2004 story of the Boston Red Sox is a great one in terms of an underdog story. Even if you’re not a Red Sox fan, this story represents a very specific time in baseball and tells the story of how this iconic team broke a curse that had existed since 1918. If your kid is just starting to get into baseball, this documentary series might seem like ancient history; after all, 2004 was more than 20 years ago. And yet, this particular season for many of us feels very recent and still relevant.

Who doesn’t love trick shots? This 30 for 30 ESPN doc is all about a group of five guys who were former college roommates who created a sports comedy entertainment phenomenon. Focused on trick shots and betting, this doc is 100% for older kids. But if you’ve got a teen who is into sports and loves to joke around, this is a great, quirky documentary focused on male friendship, humor, and creating something nobody has ever done before.

Everybody is obsessed with Travis Kelce, but his brother Jason Kelce might be the more interesting of the siblings, at least as an athlete. The 2023 documentary film chronicles the 2022 Philadelphia Eagles season, with a specific focus on Kelce. The main tension here is whether or not Kelce will retire from the NFL. Weird topic for kids? Well, for tweens and teens interested in unpacking the real-deal toll of being in the NFL, there’s something smartly educational about this. You may be young and obsessed with football now, but life is long.

Not technically a documentary, this is a docudrama based on the true story of Ray McElrathbey, who deals with a ton of family adversity and racism. Set in the early 2000s, McElrathbey’s story is inspiring and very family-oriented. Again, this one might be for older kids, but the script is from Nick Santora of Reacher and Sopranos fame, so there’s a breezy and very focused feeling to this movie.

Here’s another docudrama that is based on a real-life movement in India, centered on teenagers and skateboarding culture. In the film, a young girl named Prerna (Rachel Sanchita Gupta) finds purpose and belonging through skateboarding. The film is a heartwarming coming-of-age movie, but watching it with your kid means you’re also giving them a dose of contemporary history. The production for the film also worked very closely with rural villages in India to make sure it accurately portrayed the culture and struggles of teenagers.

A great one to watch with your aspiring skateboarding kid, or maybe a kid who isn’t sure what their athletic interest might be.

One of the greatest athletes of our time is also the subject of a one-of-a-kind docuseries. Released in 2024, Simone Biles Rising is all about the gymnast’s comeback. The fact that Biles has been so transparent about her mental health has been a groundbreaking part of the conversations about young athletes. As both a role model and someone who is part of living history, Biles is a figure that should inspire conversation with your curious athlete.

This 10-part documentary changed everything back in 2020. However, at this point, The Last Dance — which tells the story of one of the greatest periods of the Chicago Bulls — almost feels vintage. Chances are, for certain parents, you didn’t have a kid old enough to watch this documentary nearly seven years ago. And, if you’re of the generation that lived through the Bulls’ 1990s dynasty, then you owe it to share that history with your kid.

Not everything about Michael Jordan and his teammates is admirable, to be clear. But the thing about some great sports history is that it can be messy.

Focused on the 2024 X Games, The Rise: Gold Medal Girls of the X Games focuses on four teen athletes, Arisa Trew, Shiloh Catori, Reese Nelson, and Jada Ward. Those are all skateboarders, and that’s just the most recent season. More broadly, The Rise covers all sorts of women’s sports, from skating to the WNBA. If you have a young woman looking for some new role models, you can’t miss with the various seasons of The Rise.

You can really start anywhere with this excellent docuseries. But the most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained is focused on the 2024 Tour de France. Obviously, the famous bicycle race has existed since 1903, but it’s really only recently that we could actually document this incredible event. Even the least sporty kid in the world can get excited about people using their bodies to propel a bicycle forward. And the most sporty kids will have trouble wrapping their mind around the sheer effort it takes to traverse 2,200 miles over 24 days over some of the hilliest terrain on Earth.

The most recent season of Tour de France: Unchained, released in 2025, is now the last season of this docuseries. The real Tour de France hasn’t gone anywhere, of course. In fact, it’s happening right now. Meaning if you get your kid excited enough, you can watch the 2026 Tour de France as it’s happening. Or watch a little contemporary Tour de France, then go back and watch Unchained on Netflix.
