#7934. Best Gifts For Kids 2026: 43 Picks Blowing Up The Mom Group Chats

From a kid-safe saw (yes, really) to a screen-free telephone “club,” these are the picks blowing up our mom group chats.

It happens like clockwork every fall: Our mom group chats turn into one long stream of links. “Is your kid asking for this, too?” “Is it sold out??” “Ordering now; better safe than sorry!” IYKYK, and if you’re behind, well, we’ve got you.

Our editors pooled our mom group chats to parse through all the convos and conjecture about what our kids want this year, and we came up with a list of kids’ gifts real moms are actually buying (or have already procured and stuffed in a secret hiding place). There’s the landline for kids that you’ve surely been seeing all over your social media feeds, a play saw that won’t cut little fingers, a balance board that’s sneaky good for everyone in the house, and much more. There’s guaranteed to be something for every kind of kid on this list.

Keep scrolling for the gifts every mom we know is talking about.

For the baby or toddler on your holiday list, a Lovevery Play Kit is genuinely one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each kit is developmentally designed by experts for a specific age and stage, so every single toy inside has a real purpose and actually supports what that child’s brain is working on right now. The Free Spirit Kit is designed for older toddlers exploring independence, creativity, and imaginative play, and it comes with everything from open-ended building materials to pretend play pieces that grow with them well beyond the holiday season. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

The Sticki Rolls capsule series has absolutely taken over my daughter’s friend group, so she will lose her mind when she sees Series 3 under the tree. Each roll is a peel-and-stick experience that reveals collectible band stickers inside, and the trading, collecting, and comparing with friends has become a whole social event in itself. They are the kind of small, inexpensive gift that delivers an enormous reaction, which is the ideal holiday gift math. It’s the perfect stocking stuffer or add-on for any kid who is deep in the sticker and collectible era right now! — Katie Garrity

This is the holiday gift that every parent who is trying to delay handing their kid a smartphone needs to know about. The Tin Can is a Wi-Fi landline designed specifically for kids, with no screen, no apps, no social media, no browser, and no strangers getting through. You control the approved contact list from the app, kids can call friends and family with real voice calls, and there is even a free Can-to-Can plan so two Tin Can kids can call each other for free with no subscription required. My daughter loves it and I love that she gets the independence of being able to call her people without me handing over the entire internet to do it. — Katie Garrity

This is such an ideal holiday toy for me! It's physical but can be done inside, it's not made of plastic, it doesn't have noise or lights, and... I can use it too after the kids go to bed. Also you don't have to wrap it. Really, can you ask for anything more? — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

The Melissa & Doug Cheery Lane House is the kind of gift that becomes the centerpiece of playtime for years — it is a beautifully detailed wooden dollhouse play set with colorful, cheerful design that sparks hours of open-ended storytelling and creative play without a single battery or screen required. Melissa & Doug has been the gold standard in wooden toys and imaginative play for decades, and this set delivers on every bit of that quality and craftsmanship. — Katie Garrity

The Noodoll Ricespud Hot Potato is a tiny, perfectly rendered little potato plush that is so absurd and so cute at the same time that it is genuinely impossible not to love it. It is soft, squishy, palm-sized, and has the most deadpan little potato face that somehow communicates everything. It’s the kind of completely unhinged gift that costs almost nothing, takes up zero space in a stocking, and becomes the most talked-about thing under the tree because nobody expected a potato and yet here we all are. — Katie Garrity

The ChompSaw is the coolest thing I have seen for kids who want to actually make things. It is a real, functional saw designed specifically for children with a safety guard that prevents the blade from cutting skin but still cuts wood, foam, and cardboard perfectly, which means she gets the genuine satisfaction of building and creating without me hovering anxiously over every cut. It’s designed for kids 4 and up, requires zero power tools or adult intervention once they gets the hang of it, and the independent building projects it unlocks are genuinely impressive. — Katie Garrity

I love this toy because it combines two really common kid interests: building things and dinosaurs. I got this set for my twin neice and nephew and they have gotten so much (QUIET, SOLO) play time from this set. This set allows you to make three different dinosauts — T-rex, pterodactyl, brontosaurus — and they make them over and over again. It's hands-on and it uses their brains, I couldn't ask for more. — Sarah Aswell

My daughter has been asking to learn to sew and this is the perfect place to start. The Hug is a beginner-friendly kids’ sewing machine that uses yarn instead of thread, making it safe, easy, and genuinely manageable for little hands without the frustration of rethreading a needle every five minutes. It has a built-in safety finger guard, LED lighting, and comes with a full sewing kit so she can start creating immediately right out of the box. — Katie Garrity

I have a soccer obsessed kid; specifically, he wants to play goalie all the time. We practice every. Single. Day. And he always wants more time and more kicks to block. This soccer launcher has been so fun. It will fire on a five-second timer or if you clap three times, and you can adjust the height it launches at too. It's a great "big" gift for the soccer loving kid in your life. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

K-Pop and cool fashion dolls in the same box is basically a guaranteed win. The K-Pop Demon Hunters 3-pack features three fully styled dolls with incredible detail in their outfits, accessories, and overall aesthetic that feels genuinely fresh and different from anything else in the doll aisle right now. Each doll has her own distinct look and personality, and the whole set comes with the kind of intricate styling details that a kid who loves fashion, music, and K-Pop culture will absolutely obsess over. — Katie Garrity

Magnetic tiles are one of those gifts that never get old, and a 132-piece set is the kind of haul that opens up a whole new level of what they can build. The Sunny Auntie tiles are compatible with other major magnetic tile brands so they can add to an existing collection, the pieces are thick, sturdy, and safe with rounded edges and no sharp corners, and the variety of shapes in the set means endless architectural possibilities from simple towers to elaborate castles and everything in between. — Katie Garrity

This collab between Melissa & Doug and the iconic Van Leeuwen Ice Cream is the most delightful play set, and the little ones on your holiday list are going to absolutely love it! It is a fully detailed pretend play ice cream counter inspired by Van Leeuwen’s gorgeous aesthetic, complete with scoopable play ice cream, cones, toppings, and all the tools needed for the most imaginative scoop shop experience. — Katie Garrity

If you have been anywhere near a toy store, a bookstore, or the internet in the last year you already know that Jellycat has completely taken over, and this little Scottie Dog in his cozy winter jumper is exactly why. The softness is genuinely unmatched, the details are ridiculously charming, and every single Jellycat somehow manages to have more personality than a stuffed animal has any right to. My daughter because she has been asking for a Jellycat, and a dog in a tiny Christmas sweater felt like the obvious and correct choice. — Katie Garrity

My 8-year-old niece loved this pen creation station. Craft kits feel like they're back in a big way this year, and I love that this one is fun during the making and leaves you with usable pens she can take to school, and a fun little storage locker for her desk in her room. It's just little girl gift gold. — Katie McPherson

Knuffle Bunny is a full cultural moment right now, and if your kid has read Mo Willems’ beloved picture book series, getting the actual official stuffed animal is going to completely send them. The Gund version is beautifully made with that signature floppy, scrappy, well-loved look that matches the book illustrations perfectly, and the softness is exactly what you want from a toy that is going to become a forever comfort companion. — Katie Garrity

The combination of Bluey and the Scribble Scrubbie concept is genuinely my daughter’s two favorite hobbies all in one. The Scribble Scrubbie pets are washable toy figures that kids can color with markers, scrub clean, and color all over again, which means the creative play never runs out. The Bluey version gives you Bluey and Bingo to color and decorate, which is going to be an absolutely unhinged amount of fun for any kid obsessed with the show. — Katie Garrity

For the kid who already has a Nugget and is completely obsessed with Minecraft, this cover set is going to make the holidays. The Minecraft collab brings the iconic blocky aesthetic to the covers in a way that is genuinely cool and immediately recognizable to any fan. It transforms an already beloved piece of furniture into the ultimate Minecraft hangout zone without any new hardware required, just swap the covers and watch your kid completely lose their mind. — Katie Garrity

We've tried a few different audio players over the years and the Yoto is the one that has really stuck for my son. He uses it every night to listen to a story while he drifts off, and he looks forward to the Yoto Daily podcast with Jake too. This generation of Yoto has so many features I love, from the built-in night light (no more traveling with both!), to the new green button on the side that makes it easy to toggle through favorite stories without carrying along their cards. This is a fabulous gift idea that'll truly be used and loved for many years to come (ours has been THROWN many times during toddler tantrums and still works like a dream). — Katie McPherson

This is a craft kit and a fidget toy in one, which is basically the dream combo for a kid who can’t sit still. The kit comes with 101 scented squishy beads in flower, heart, round, and star shapes, plus five reusable elastic bracelets and a beading needle, so my daughter can make a bracelet, squish it, take it apart, and start over. It’s a screen-free gift that keeps her hands busy for hours, and I’m not above admitting I’ll probably end up making a bracelet too! — Katie Garrity

These are just the cutest overalls that remind me of what I wore when I was a kid. They're designed by Sergio Hudson, who did a special collaboration with Osh Kosh this winter. I love the pop of color, I love the stripes, I love it all. And I know your kid will, too. — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief

This is the gift that keeps my daughter happily occupied without a screen in sight, and the starter set means there’s no scrambling to figure out what else you need. You just set a Tonie character on top of the box and it plays stories, songs, and adventures, and it’s simple enough that she runs the whole thing herself. It’s become part of our daily routine, and it’s the kind of present kids keep reaching for long after the wrapping paper is gone! — Katie Garrity

The “more is more” customizing trend is real in our house, and these let my daughter decorate everything she owns without a single bottle of glue. Each pack has 15 glossy, 3D resin charms in pink kawaii creatures, sweet treats, and whimsical icons that peel off the backing and stick to anything flat, like her phone case, journal, or water bottle. It’s a small, inexpensive gift that gets a big reaction, and I fully expect to find a tiny charm stuck to something I own by January. — Katie Garrity

This new set from Magna-Tiles takes everything my daughter loves about building with Magna-Tiles and adds ball runs, which means she gets to engineer a track and then immediately test whether it works. The set has 78 magnetic pieces plus two racing balls, including a trapdoor, a slide, and curved and short rails, so she can build multi-level raceways with tight turns and big drops. It works with any Magna-Tiles she already owns, and it’s a screen-free gift that teaches cause and effect while she thinks she’s just playing. — Katie Garrity

There’s SNOW much to love about this limited-edition Snoopy purse, which is designed to look like a mini puffer coat with a quilted detail and a chain strap. It comes in a pretty Swiss blue, closes with a magnetic snap, and is part of Janie and Jack’s winter PEANUTS collection, so it’s guaranteed to make her whole cozy-weather outfit feel complete. It’s small and special enough to fit all her tiny treasures! — Katie Garrity

I've had my eye on the Nex for a long time, and I wish I'd gotten one sooner! We love gaming as a family and it makes me so happy to have the Nex on the mantle for rainy or cold days when it's zero fun to be outside, but we neeeeed to move around and burn energy. It's gaming with way less guilt and feels like a family activity we all look forward to. And yeah, Fruit Ninja is just way more fun when you're karate chopping with your whole chest rather than getting finger burn swiping like crazy. — Katie McPherson

I got this set for my new niece, and I still cannot get over how perfect it is! It’s soft and airy, thanks to the 100% cotton gauze, and that hand-drawn tulip print? Stahhhp, it’s so charming. It’s a good thing my kids are no longer little or I would literally be buying up every single thing on this site. I think this would make the sweetest gift for any little girl in your life. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This new board game has everything I like: easy rules, really beautiful design, and short game play (around a half-hour). I also love 2-player games that I can either play with one kid or with my partner. The premise is very simple: build a 3D volcano with certain features before your opponent does. I love that this can be very simple or very strategic — there's also an expansion set that bring the game up to 4 players. — Sarah Aswell

For the little racer who’s obsessed with Mario Kart, this officially licensed slot car set brings the game to the living room floor, with Mario and Yoshi going head to head on a 9-foot track with a built-in lap counter to crown the winner. It’s made for kids ages 3 and up and gives two players a screen-free way to duke it out, which is the kind of gift that gets pulled out over and over. — Katie Garrity

If you have a kid who refuses to come inside until her fingers are numb, this is the snowsuit that lets her stay out there, because it’s waterproof and breathable, so she stays dry whether she’s sledding, skiing, or face-planting into a snowbank. It’s built with real snowsport details, including several pockets and adjustability, so it can keep up with a growing kid through the whole winter. It's a splurge, but it’s the one piece of winter gear that makes getting her out the door a lot less of a battle. — Katie Garrity

Anyone else have a Grinch-obsessed child? The Grinch with a light-up heart is basically the holiday plush equivalent of a happy ending, and she already quotes the movie every December. It’s an 18-inch, soft and fuzzy Grinch with a glowing heart on his chest, which makes it a great cuddle buddy and a night-time companion all season. Made for ages 2 and up, it’s the kind of gift that instantly becomes a holiday tradition (and gets a spot on the couch until New Year’s). — Katie Garrity

Now, this a video game I can say yes to without a second thought, with Bluey and Bingo finding Dad’s old camera and snapping photos around the show’s famous spots, then saving everything in a scrapbook she can decorate with stickers. It has local co-op so a second player can join in and strike a pose, plus no in-game purchases and no online play, which is the kind of kid-friendly setup parents love. The Deluxe Edition adds the Here Come the Grannies bonus content, extra dress-up items, and a digital art book, and the “For Real Life” activity ideas even get her playing away from the screen. — Katie Garrity

OK so... I want one of these, too. My two tween girls are VERY into fidget toys and squishies, so we have a lot in my house. My favorite one to steal is this butter block. It's adorable on my desk and great to squeeze during meetings and phone calls. But also great for the kids they're meant for. And fits in a stocking! — Sarah Aswell

For the toddler in your life who already knows every word to Ms. Rachel’s songs, this Yoto card puts the whole debut album on a screen-free player, with all 23 tracks, including “Icky Sticky Bubblegum,” “I Love a Rainbow,” “Big Feelings,” and a few classics like “The Wheels on the Bus.” Kids just pop the card into a Yoto Player or Yoto Mini to hear it, which means a dance party can happen without anyone handing over a phone. It’s $14.99, made for ages 1 and up, and the card launches Nov. 12, so it’s available to preorder now, which makes it a perfect stocking stuffer for any family that already has a Yoto. — Katie Garrity

For the kid on your list who’s obsessed with Star Wars, this 13-inch remote control walker is basically a movie scene they can drive around the living room, with a Mandalorian and Grogu figure riding in the cockpit. It really walks, runs, and turns with a 2.4 GHz remote, and it comes loaded with LED lights, laser cannon sounds, and real Star Wars audio clips, so every trip across the floor feels like a battle. It’s made for ages 8 and up and is a Walmart exclusive, and honestly the walker looks cool enough on a shelf that parents will be tempted to play too. — Katie Garrity

My 11-year-old kid is so hard to buy presents for. She's kind of not into toys anymore, but she's not ready to go over to the realm of all clothes and self-care and novels yet. Well... when I saw this Chia Pet bison... I know that she would have at least one thing under the tree that she absolutely loved. I love that this has a bit of a "toy" feel, but it's also cool room decor. — Sarah Aswell

These 14-inch dolls are incredily cute and well-made. I love that the dolls look like actual normal girls without exaggerated or sexualized features and I love that the price point adds a good option for families that can't drop three digits for an American Girl Dolls. There are also lots of great accessories available, also at reasonable prices! — Sarah Aswell

I genuinely would put these on and wear them myself if I could, but I suppose I’ll just have to settle for watching my niece romp around in them. I love that these are fully waterpoof but also lightweight and flexible enough that kids don’t feel like they’re walking around wearing cinder blocks. Another great feature is the grippy outsole to help keep little ones from slipping while they’re exploring on wet ground. And they’re made from natural rubber, so totally non-toxic! — Julie Sprankles

Clickeez are tiny character keycaps that click and clack like a real mechanical keyboard, and the Series 3 Bubble Pops theme has a softer, quieter click that’s almost as satisfying as the surprise of seeing which ones you get. The Mega Pack comes with a keyboard-shaped case and 12 characters to display and swap in and out, plus there are 70+ characters to hunt for, including rare surprises, so she can build a collection one click at a time. It’s made for ages 6 and up and is a great screen-free gift for any kid who loves to collect (and click)! — Katie Garrity

The details in this LEGO build are amazing, from the chain-driven V* engine compressor to the functional steering and suspension. Honestly, I got this car for my (grown, adult) brother and a different, simpler Fast and Furious car for my nephew to build along side him. I love how many brain-building, screenless hours of fun these sets provide — and then you can watch the movie after. — Sarah Aswell

I mean, the title really explains everything. This shoots farts at people. I fully admit that I bought this for my brother's children and not for mine, and they played with it for *hours*. There was so much laughter, and honestly, the smell is not that bad for the adults in the room (although we did kick them outside). I think they ran more than when they play sports. — Sarah Aswell

Is there anything cuter than a denim jacket on a child? No there is not. Enter this adorable teddy fleece-lined jacket that you just know your kid will love. It's cozy, classic and totally show-stopping. — Kate Auletta

Every mom knows that it’s the absolute worst when your little one is feeling under the weather... and it can especially wreak havoc on sleep. This special Gund bear helps kids fall asleep by doubling as a sound machine with nine gentle modes. It even comes with a bedtime story! It’s created to kind of perfectly fit against a little one’s chest as they bring it in for a, well, bear hug, and that squeeze activates the soothing sounds. Kids will love getting it as a gift, but Mom might love it even more. — Julie Sprankles

#7932. Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he currently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he says. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

How's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

For the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

In terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

So I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

But thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

And certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

It's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a big focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

That's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

And I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some new young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really important to them.

Once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

It's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

Many salvias can tough it out through fall, but even these easygoing plants need a helping hand in winter. Make time for our smart overwintering tips to protect these iconic favorites

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As a seasoned gardener, if you ask me to name an easy-to-grow flowering perennial that returns reliably year after year, salvia would be at the top of my list. In my own garden, my ‘Hot Lips’ shrubby salvia shrugs off summer drought, asks for very little maintenance, and blooms generously from late spring through to November. Their nectar-rich flower spikes are magnets for hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies, drenching borders in rich purples, electric blues, hot pinks, and velvety crimsons.

Yet, despite their tough and easygoing nature, winter is the one season where salvias do need a bit of care and attention. The genus Salvia is vast, encompassing over a thousand species of annuals, woody sub-shrubs, and herbaceous perennials from regions as diverse as cold alpine meadows, dry Mediterranean hillsides, and tropical cloud forests. Because their natural habitats differ dramatically, their winter cold tolerance does, too. What protects a hardy meadow sage in New England will not save a tender Mexican bush salvia during a sudden polar snap. So winter salvia care needs to be adapted accordingly.

Taking action now, in this narrow window between autumn's close and winter's first freeze, is critical. Winter damage can happen fast, and yet knowing how to winterize salvias is surprisingly easy. By understanding your variety's cold tolerance and taking action fast, you can help prime your salvia in winter. Here’s how to easily guide your garden favorites through to next spring, so you can enjoy their lush, vibrant blooms for years to come.

The precise winter protection required will depend on where you live and the type of salvia you are growing. Some are cold-hardy perennials, while others are tender, frost-sensitive tropicals. So successful winterizing begins with identifying growth habit and hardiness classification. Deciduous herbaceous salvias like meadow sage (S. nemorosa cultivars like Caradonna and May Night) and woodland sage (S. pratensis) are cold-hardy in USDA hardiness zones 3-8. These perennials die back after hard frosts, resting safely underground before surging back in spring. They need little winter protection beyond good drainage and light insulation.

Shrubby, semi-hardy salvias (S. greggii and S. microphylla) occupy a middle ground, thriving in zones 6-9. These semi-evergreen sub-shrubs develop woody stems that can be damaged by sudden cold snaps or damp winter soils. In colder microclimates within these zones, they require protective mulching and shelter from wet winds. Finally, tender subtropical and tropical salvias, including velvet-flowered Amistad and Mexican bush sage (S. leucantha), flourish only in frost-free zones 8-11. These are large, bushy salvias that are killed by hard winter freezes, so in cooler zones, they require extra winter protection.

Before you begin, test your soil moisture levels and check that water drains away readily after rain. The XLUX Long Probe Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon is a great dual soil moisture and pH diagnostic probe, giving instant readings to help you identify waterlogged soil pockets before the ground freezes. Once your soil is identified, you’re ready to take action. Here we clarify when to cut your salvias back, how to protect the roots from cold and wet conditions, and how to ensure you see your jewel-toned flowering favorites again next year.

When salvias start looking ragged, the natural impulse is to reach for the bypass pruners and shear everything back to a tidy clump. This could be the most damaging mistake you make. Many perennial salvias (especially semi-woody and herbaceous varieties) have hollow, straw-like stems. Pruning these down in late fall leaves those open tubes exposed to the elements. Rain and melting snow funnel down the stems and collect at the base, causing crown rot and fungal decay in freeze-thaw cycles.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It’s best to leave these old stems, faded flower spikes, and withered foliage in place to keep driving rain away from the vulnerable center. This dried top growth also traps air, forming an insulating buffer that protects the dormant buds huddled around the crown. So resist all heavy pruning until early spring, when fresh shoots begin pushing through the soil. Even if you live in a warm-winter area, it’s still best to leave major pruning until spring. The only fall cuts you should make are removing broken or diseased stems. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, when removing broken salvia stems.

Whenever I mulch plants for winter, I think of tucking a blanket around a sleeping child. Mulching salvias as cold weather is coming offers a layer of winter protection. When you apply mulch before the first hard freeze, you protect the root crown from severe cold and freeze-heave. In regions with fluctuating winter weather, bare soil expands and contracts, pushing shallow crowns up and exposing roots. Fully hardy salvia don’t need much winter protection, but a light mulch won’t hurt. When it comes to the semi-hardy salvias, however, mulching is a must to help overwintering plants.

The type of mulch, and how you apply it, are critical to avoid trapping moisture around the plant. Avoid dense, heavy materials like wet grass clippings, uncomposted manure, or thick leaf mold, which pack down and suffocate the plant. Instead, apply 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of loose, breathable mulch such as shredded pine bark, clean wheat straw, dry bracken, or horticultural grit. Keep it 2-3 inches (5-8cm) from the stems to avoid trapping moisture and inviting crown rot. Buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot for a loose yet insulating blanket.

Cold isn’t necessarily fatal for salvia plants in winter. But too much water will take out your salvias faster than a freeze. Native to sun-drenched Mediterranean climes, salvias demand sharp drainage. When sluggish drainage keeps soil saturated, oxygen is pushed out of the roots, leaving the crown vulnerable to fungal diseases. You’ll want to take steps to avoid poorly drained soil and winter wetness for any type of salvia.

If your garden has heavy clay soil, take action now before winter sets in. Gently scrape away decomposing leaves, as wet leaf mats retain moisture over the crown. Work a handful of coarse horticultural grit, sand or perlite into the soil surface around the plant to speed up surface runoff. Back to the Roots Organic Perlite from Walmart is a great option for improving soil aeration and drainage around salvias. For container-grown plants, elevate the pots off cold, wet patio slabs. Use terracotta pot feet, pot toes, or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear of standing water.

If your salvia are tender varieties like Amistad or S. leucantha, treat them like the cold vulnerable plants that they are. Sub-tropical salvias can’t tolerate hard frosts or frozen soil. Leaving them unprotected in northern yards guarantees root death. Fortunately, tender salvias overwinter indoors with minimal fuss, provided you bring them into shelter before the first hard frost blackens foliage. If your tender salvias are in pots, trim the longest branches back by half, then move to an unheated garage, frost-free shed, cold frame, or cool porch, and keep at 35-45°F (2-7°C).

For tender salvias in beds, carefully dig up the root ball with a spade, keeping plenty of soil around the roots. Place into a plastic nursery container, backfill loosely with dry potting mix, and move it undercover. Use plant caddies such as the Bloem Plant Caddy from The Home Depot to wheel larger container-based salvias into the garage with zero strain or back pain. The goal is to keep the plant dormant. Water sparingly: just a cup or two a month keeps the root ball from drying out.

Even with meticulous winter care, an unseasonal polar vortex or prolonged freeze can challenge borderline-hardy salvias. Taking a few semi-ripe salvia cuttings provides a terrific insurance policy. Select healthy, non-flowering or semi-ripe shoots (or snip the flower tip off a vigorous stem). Take a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) cutting below a leaf node. Strip the leaves from the bottom half, leaving 2-3 pairs of small leaves at the top. Dip into a rooting hormone such as HydroDynamics Clonex Rooting Gel from Amazon, to seal cut stems and trigger root growth. Insert the cuttings into small pots filled with a 50/50 mix of sterile seed compost and perlite.

Water gently, then place a clear plastic dome or bag over the pot to maintain humidity. Set your baby cuttings on a bright, warm windowsill, but out of direct sunlight. They should root within 3-4 weeks. Keep them lightly watered through winter, and pinch the tips in late winter to encourage bushy growth. Just bear in mind that rooting will be slower now than it would be with cuttings taken in late summer or early fall. Grown on a sunny indoor windowsill or greenhouse bench through winter, your salvia babies will hopefully be ready to plant out next May.

By the time spring arrives, you’ll be eager for warmer days and fresh growth (and so will your salvias!). As sunny afternoons begin warming the soil, check your overwintered salvias for vibrant green shoots emerging. That is your signal that winter danger has passed. You can then prune away old standing stems just above the fresh growth nodes. If you have woody salvias, spring is the time to shape the plant. Cut it back by a third to clean up the shrub. Spring is also the time to pull back protective mulches and reintroduce sheltered container plants to outdoor sunshine. With their crowns preserved through the cold months, your salvias will soon be rewarding you with months of lush and lively color.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7929. This ‘unhinged’ advice for toddler moms is actually pretty genius

We've all earned our stripes, and sometimes there's nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 13, 2026

Toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in. Some came from toddler room teachers, longtime nannies and even doctors. Most came from moms who’ve logged countless hours negotiating with toddlers and consulting their pediatricians. We’ve all earned our stripes, and sometimes there’s nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

Many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged. And certainly no one’s judging.

Anyone who has turned around in a parking lot to find an empty space where a small person used to be knows this particular brand of panic. The thread’s most-liked reply, with nearly 18,000 hearts, went straight at the escape artist problem, and the moms underneath it kept the ideas coming.

Credit: @thriving_out_of_spite, @norcalcaro and @sksargeant via Threads

One mom’s solution doubled as entertainment.

(If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.)

Toddler palates are a moving target. The food they inhaled one day is suddenly disgusting the next. A couple of moms found that a little creative branding goes a long way, at the table and beyond.

Brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

When a meltdown hits, plenty of moms agreed the first move is regulating yourself. Toddlers take their emotional cues from us, so the calmer we stay, the faster they come back down.

From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

That sniff trick is a cousin of the viral “Jessica” trick, where a parent interrupts a meltdown by calmly calling for someone who isn’t there. Pediatrician Dr. Madison Szar told Motherly that “What’s that smell?” works just as well, since the surprise is what breaks the loop. Bonus points for the deep breaths.

And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.

Then there are the white lies. One bedtime fib stood out as particularly clever.

Having raised two kids, one in college and one in high school, I can attest that I lied to them. A lot. The car won’t start unless you’re buckled. It’s against the law to take your shoes off in the store. The toy store is closing, so we have to leave now. I promise you they are both 100% trustworthy, honest people.

When I was a new mom, just 21 and wildly out of my depth, I had a mentor with a toddler of her own. A yoga teacher who became a mom in her early 40s, she was a free spirit who didn’t mother through the lens of anyone else’s scrutiny. It was wild and refreshing.

She was willing to be inconvenienced so her son could explore and held firm when exploring teetered toward danger. She also leaned into the absurdity. At one point she’d somehow acquired a shopping cart, and when her son got grumpy, she’d load him in with a rug, some toys and their cat (I’m not kidding) and march around the neighborhood with the dog following behind.

Toddlers are ridiculous, and we all know it. Sometimes you have to meet the moment with the same.

Here's how I reclaimed my time without compromising care for my little ones.

#7928. Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

What Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

She doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

#7927. 6 Gardening Jobs You Must Finish Before the First Hard Freeze – Or You’ll Regret it in Spring

A hard freeze can do damage you won't see until spring, from cracked pots to rotten bulbs. These tasks can't wait for winter – and the window is closing fast, so hurry!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even in November, backyards can look like they got some time left, perhaps with a few late-season tomatoes still clinging to the vine and container tropicals green on the patio. But all it takes is one hard freeze, dropping overnight temperatures with a day or two’s notice. Suddenly, tender leaves turn black and crops are ruined. What’s worse is that much of the damage stays hidden until spring.

You’ll only discover a split copper pipe when you turn on the hose in April, or realize you lost your prized dahlia tubers when green shoots fail to emerge. Sure, not every chore needs to be tackled now. Routine pruning and bed edging can wait until late winter. However, certain tasks carry a hard deadline set by the weather: this includes anything involving overwintering plants, as well as plumbing fixtures that hold water.

In some yards, this deadline has already passed, and in others, it's coming up this week. Completing the following tasks before temperatures plunge can save you hundreds of dollars in expensive winter damage, and keeps everything in the best shape for spring. Here’s how to make sure your garden emerges strong and healthy next year.

Understanding the difference between a light frost and a hard freeze can give you the lead time you need. Growers sometimes talk about frosts and freezes interchangeably, but the differences matter. A light frost occurs when air temperatures hover right at the freezing threshold (32°F / 0°C), forming ice crystals on leaf surfaces. While tender annuals like basil and coleus blacken quickly at this temperature, cold-tolerant vegetables like kale shrug it off (and even taste better).

A hard freeze is more aggressive. It occurs when ambient temperatures drop to 28°F (-2°C) or lower and remain there for several hours. At this depth of cold, ice crystals form inside plant cell walls, bursting cellular membranes and killing unhardened woody stems. A hard freeze also freezes water inside pipes, outdoor faucets, and irrigation lines. True frozen ground, where soil hardens into an impenetrable crust, usually develops weeks later after sustained sub-freezing weather.

Northern gardens are often done by November, while milder regions may still have several weeks. Because first-freeze dates are geographical moving targets, your regional location dictates your timeline. Gardeners in northern USDA hardiness zones 3-5 often face hard freezes by mid-October, while those in milder zones 7-9 may not see temperatures dip below 28°F until late December or January. This can help prevent panicking too early – or waiting too late.

Don’t wait for a freeze warning to assemble your gear. Keeping insulated spigot covers, garden forks, frost fabric, and storage crates on hand now ensures you can secure your yard quickly when the first blue whistler rolls in. To help you track things, it’s also a good idea to have a thermometer on standby. The TempPro TempAir 500 FT Indoor/Outdoor Thermometer, available from Amazon, can help you to stay one step ahead of any overnight shocks. Then you’re ready to tackle these tasks…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One frost can ruin tomatoes, peppers, eggplants, and basil. Even near-freezing temperatures in the mid-30s can cause chilling injury to peppers and eggplants, dulling skin quality and introducing rot spots. So strip your vines of all mature crops before freezing weather arrives. Use sharp scissors or snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Garden Snips from Amazon.

Gather every ripe tomato, along with full-sized green tomatoes that have developed a glossy, pale-green sheen. Placed in a cardboard box indoors at room temperature, mature green fruits will ripen off the vine over the next few weeks. Leave small, hard fruits behind, as they lack the maturity to ripen. Pull up basil plants to process into pesto or dry indoors.

However, you can leave cool-season brassicas and root crops where they are. Collards, Brussels sprouts, kale, carrots, and parsnips tolerate temperatures well below 28°F (-2°C). The cold triggers these hardy crops to convert complex starches into plant sugars, which can help them taste sweeter after frost.

In regions with cold winters (typically zones 7 and colder), tender summer-flowering bulbs, tubers, and corms won’t survive in freezing ground. Leaving dahlias, cannas, calla lilies, caladiums, gladioli, and tuberous begonias in the soil too long, and the fleshy storage organs will freeze, decompose, and turn to mush. Dahlias and cannas benefit from waiting until an initial light frost blackens the foliage. (Tuberous begonias are more tender and often need to get lifted earlier as the leaves yellow.)

Once that light freeze hits, don’t wait for the ground to freeze solid. Cut black stems back to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). Carefully insert a garden fork into the earth, at least 12 inches (30cm) from the main stalk to avoid impaling the tubers. Gently pry the root clump upward. Shake off loose soil, and allow the tubers to cure in a dry, frost-free garage for a few days.

Then gently pack in cardboard boxes filled with dry peat moss, vermiculite, or wood shavings. You can buy Plantonix Premium Vermiculite Bliss from Walmart to help protect dahlia and canna tubers against humidity spikes and fungal rots. Store in a dark, cool space between 40-50°F (4-10°C). Where winters are mild (zone 8 and warmer), dahlias can stay in the ground, provided soil drains freely and is protected with mulch.

Plumbing and outdoor water features carry the highest financial risk when a hard freeze arrives. Water expands by about 9% when it turns to ice. Even if your home features modern "frost-free" outdoor hose spigots, leaving a garden hose attached prevents the internal valve from draining properly. The pipe inside the wall can split, unnoticed until it leaks in spring. So uncouple every hose, stretch them out on a gentle incline to drain residual water, and roll them up for indoor storage.

If your home has an interior shutoff valve for exterior spigots, close it now. Open the outside tap to bleed the line, and then secure an insulated foam faucet cover over the fixture. You can get Frost King FC1 Foam Faucet Covers from Walmart in double packs. Drip lines can usually be drained by opening the end caps. In-ground lawn sprinkler systems require compressed air to blow all standing water out of the pipes, manifold valves, and pop-up heads. Too much air pressure can crack pipes and heads, so if you don't know your system, winterizing sprinklers is better left to a pro.

Anything holding standing water is at risk. Drain cast concrete, ceramic, and stone water fountains. Cover them with waterproof tarps to prevent pooled water from freezing and cracking the masonry. For bird baths, stone bowls will split under hard freezes, so store decorative basins indoors. To support backyard birds in winter, add a designated heated bird bath such as the Gesail Heated Bird Bath from Amazon. You can attach this to a decking or balcony and it’s a great depth for smaller songbirds. Alternatively, float a clean rubber ball or rubber duck on the surface of frost-safe metal basins to keep surface water moving.

Container-grown plants are far more vulnerable to cold than specimens planted in garden beds. Cold air surrounds the container on all sides, dropping potting soil temperatures up to 20°F lower than garden beds. An outdoor shrub rated hardy to your zone might still freeze and die if left unprotected in a pot. Roots in a pot sit above ground, with cold reaching them from the sides as well as the top. They're also less cold-hardy than the stems above them.

Tropical plants, potted citrus, pelargoniums, and tender patio perennials should be moved indoors once nighttime temperatures hover around 50°F (10°C). Before anything goes inside, inspect leaf undersides and stem junctions for hitchhiking pests like aphids, mealybugs, and spider mites, as well as webs or anything sticky. Wash the foliage with a gentle stream of water. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to roll heavy container citrus plants and tropicals indoors. Keep them apart from houseplants until you're sure nothing hitched a ride.

Pots left out need plants rated a zone or two hardier than your area. For hardy perennials, boxwoods, and dwarf conifers in large patio containers, group pots along a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall. Elevate on pot feet to ensure drainage holes remain ice-free, and wrap in burlap or bubble wrap to protect root balls from freezing solid. An unheated garage is fine for many hardy potted plants: just water them now and then so the soil doesn't dry out completely.

Fall is an ideal time for planting perennials and shrubs, but specimens tucked into borders within the last 6-8 weeks have not had long to root and establish. As freeze-thaw cycles strike, frost heave can push shallow perennial crowns and strawberry plants out of the ground. Mulch can help, but you need to time this right. Wait until after the first hard freeze has cooled the ground.

Once the top inch of soil is cold, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose organic mulch to new plantings and strawberry patches. Good options are shredded pine bark, clean wheat straw, or chopped leaves. You can buy Timberline Pine Bark Nuggets from The Home Depot. Keep it pulled back 2-3 inches (5-8cm) from plant crowns to prevent moisture buildup and winter rot.

Vulnerable shrubs require above-ground shielding. Broadleaf evergreens like boxwood, rhododendron, and cherry laurel continue to lose moisture through their leaves in winter. Combined with winter sun and wind, this can cause foliage burn. Water deeply before soil freezes. Then drive stakes into the ground around vulnerable shrubs while the soil is still workable, and fasten some burlap to form a windbreak. On old-wood bigleaf hydrangeas, use these screens to protect fragile flower buds.

Porous containers left out in freezing conditions are a common source of costly winter loss. Unglazed terracotta, ceramic pots, and composite clay planters absorb water during fall rains. When temperatures plunge below 28°F (-2°C), the moisture trapped within the clay walls expands, causing pottery to crack and split. This won’t always be obvious until spring, when a planter crumbles as soon as it is lifted.

Before freezing weather arrives, empty all unused potting soil, as a damp potting mix retains water that accelerates cracking. Scrub the inside walls with a stiff brush to remove mineral salts. For a good set of stiff bristles, buy the OXO Good Grips Heavy Duty Scrub Brush from Amazon. Allow the pottery to dry in the sun, then store the containers upside down in an unheated shed, garage, or dry basement. If planters are too heavy to move inside, empty the soil, turn them upside down on wooden blocks off the ground, and secure a waterproof tarp over them.

Take a few minutes to drain all watering cans, sprayers, and outdoor hoses, storing them where residual water cannot freeze and split their seams. Finish by scraping dried soil off spades, trowels, and hoes. Wipe the blades with a rag dipped in mineral or vegetable oil. This will prevent rust while tools sit idle over the winter months.

Some common fall chores can wait until well after the first hard freeze. In fact, tackling certain jobs too early can do more harm than good. Hold off pruning deciduous shade trees, fruit trees, and summer-blooming shrubs like panicle hydrangeas until late winter or early spring. Pruning now opens fresh wounds that cannot form protective callus tissue before a severe cold sets in, increasing the risk of injury and infection.

General border clean-up and leaf raking can also be paced out. Leaving dried flower heads, ornamental grasses, and hollow perennial stems standing in early winter provides structural interest in snowy beds. More importantly, these standing seed heads supply winter food for foraging birds like goldfinches, while hollow stems provide shelter for overwintering native bees and beneficial insects.

Finally, mulching hybrid tea roses and established perennial crowns can wait until several hard freezes have pushed plants into deep dormancy and chilled the soil. Rushing to mulch warm soil traps ground heat, delaying dormancy and encouraging tender shoots. Focus your immediate energy on plumbing, tender crops, and cold-vulnerable tubers; the rest can be tidied over the coming weekends.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7925. The Unexpected Gift That Everyone Will Be Fighting Over At Your Holiday White Elephant

Turns out, the most steal-worthy gift might also be the most practical.

White Elephant gifts fall into two categories. There’s the novelty item that gets a huge laugh, takes one triumphant lap around the room, and disappears into the black hole at the back of your closet. Then there’s the unexpected G.O.A.T everyone clamors for. It’s useful. It’s clever. It leaves everyone thinking “Why didn’t I think of that?”

This year, we’re making a case for a sleeper hit: a pack of Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries. Hear us out.

Sure, batteries might not spark the immediate razzle-dazzle of a mini karaoke machine or a candle shaped like a plate of spaghetti. But they do have something arguably more powerful: the ability to solve a future problem. These pocket-sized powerhouses keep your life going. Especially when we’re talking about the holidays.

Picture it. It’s December. The house is lit up like a regional airport runway. Your kid has acquired approximately 11 new objects that beep, flash, sing, or inexplicably do all three. Somewhere in your home, a tiny screwdriver is about to become the most important object you own.

In the midst of all this, the question hits you. Did you remember to buy batteries? Exactly. Why should you stock up on Energizer® batteries for this year’s white elephant? Let us count the ways.

There’s something deeply satisfying about having an aggressively stocked battery drawer. It’s the domestic equivalent of having a full tank of gas and remembering to defrost the chicken before 5 p.m.

Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries have a 25 year shelf life, which means your White Elephant contribution could conceivably still be hanging around when today’s toddlers are complaining about their own toddlers.

That also makes them the rare holiday gift that comes with absolutely no urgency. Nobody needs to exchange them for another size. Nobody has to smile politely while wondering whether the gift giver simply regifted the item. Nobody needs to dig it out of the back of the dresser to wear the one time the gifter comes by a year.

They call it the battery drawer for a reason. And one day, perhaps years from now, you open it in a moment of need and discover them sitting there. Cause you planned ahead.

December has a way of revealing just how much of your home is quietly powered by AA batteries.

The flameless candles? Batteries. The light-up garland? Batteries. The singing stuffed reindeer Grandma bought your child despite your explicit request for “nothing with sounds”? You better believe that thing needs batteries.

Just when you thought you were out of the woods, Christmas morning arrives and ushers in a fresh crop of tiny battery-powered overlords. Race cars. Remote controls. Games. Noise-making toys that leave you wondering whether the toy’s product designer has ever met a parent.

Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® is the #1 longest-lasting AA battery, designed to keep the devices your family relies on going and going.

Is it slightly ironic to give someone batteries that could keep their kid’s noisiest toy going and going? Yes. That’s the risk you take.

So batteries? Batteries are getting forgotten.

They are perhaps the quintessential “Oh, shoot!” holiday purchase. The thing you realize you need precisely when every store is closed, and a child is staring at you with the devastated expression of someone whose brand-new toy is apparently just a decorative object now.

Which is why Energizer® Ultimate Lithium® AA batteries make such a sneaky-good White Elephant gift. You’re not really giving someone batteries. You’re giving them the ability to skip one future panic trip to the store.

So yes, wrap up the batteries. Everyone can laugh when they’re opened. Until the snatching starts.

#7924. 32 Gifts For The Mom Who Has One Good Outfit & Wears It Everywhere

No wardrobe overhaul needed, just a few clever pieces to make her feel more put together.

Listen. Moms are juggling about a million things every minute of every day. We're bopping all over the place, half-frantic half the time, scooting kids from school to extracurriculars and keeping everyone's schedules from imploding and, and, and... the list is literally never-ending. So, yeah, maybe we reach for the same outfit or some spin on it every time we leave the house. Our unofficial uniform most days is black yoga pants and an oversized sweatshirt. And, sure, there are many days when we look like Adam Sandler's stunt double rolling through the school pickup line. Hey, whatever; it works. It's comfy and reliable.

That doesn't mean that even the most prolific outfit repeater hasn't caught a stray glimpse of herself in the mirror and thought, Hmm, my wardrobe could use a little love. Enter: these gifts. Trust, we're not here to talk anyone out of their uniform. (Respectfully, we would never.) We’re just talking about giving her a few pieces that will make her feel fresh and more put-together on the days she wants to try something different. A statement boot, a chic pullover, a bandana for a pop of print, jewelry she’ll never take off: small swaps that turn “I just threw this on” into “This is exactly the look I was going for” without a ton of effort or extra thought.

Our editors rounded up the pieces that have been reviving our go-to outfits — and confidence — lately.

This bracelet has become one of my most-worn pieces! The Nigella is a delicate, stacked look that hits that perfect sweet spot between casual enough to wear every day and special enough to feel like real jewelry. It’s the kind of gift that comes in a beautiful box, looks significantly more expensive than it is, and immediately becomes a daily staple for whoever is lucky enough to receive it. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

I’ve heard nothing but rave reviews about Rothy’s for years, but I’d never owned a pair myself. This now marks my second pair, and I wish I’d started buying them sooner. A bold shoe is such an easy way to switch up your same old outfits, and these Ivy Sneakers make a statement without trying too hard. The dark cheetah print has a soft, suede-like finish; they come with an extra pair of bright red laces for a pop of color; and they’re seriously comfy. Oh, and I LOVE that they’re knit from recycled plastic bottles! — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This is the year I got into bandanas, and I own a few Handker brand ones that have held up so well. They add a small (so not overwhelming for us black wearers) pop of color and a print, and you can wear them in so many styles on your neck alone. But they also look great in your hair, tied to a belt loop, or on your bag. They're a super affordable way to play with color and pattern, and jazz up the pieces you already own and love to wear. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

I feel way cooler than I actually am every single time I put on this jacket. Between its vintage bomber energy, fun California-inspired patches, and slightly oversized fit, it adds personality to anything you pair it with. I chose the plum color, which is literal perfection for fall and winter, and it looks equally stunning with or without the removable faux-fur collar. Also, if you’re unsure what to wear with it, Carve Designs offers outfit suggestions on their site. — Julie Sprankles

When I hear anything called "viral" I usually get suspicious, but after I tried these lovely plastic-free solid lip serums, I was a convert. These are three new Mexican dessert flavors/shades, and they are my new favorites. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

Say you're a Swiftie and love the song "The Fate of Ophelia." Or say you just really love kickass women and want to reclaim that. Then Hysteria is the brand for you. These pieces are ornate and pretty and make just about any outfit. This Ophelia necklace in particular is a showstopper. — Kate Auletta, Editor-in-Chief

This is the bag for the mom who found one outfit that works and has been wearing it on rotation since 2019. The Petal Parade Crossbody is the kind of accessory that makes a simple jeans-and-top combo look completely intentional and pulled together without requiring a single additional effort, and the floral beaded design is vibrant, joyful, and genuinely eye-catching in a way that reads as stylish rather than trying too hard. It is hands-free, the perfect size for the essentials, and the kind of bag that turns a uniform into an outfit every single time she reaches for it. Elevate the one good outfit with zero additional commitment required! — Katie Garrity

I have really found my personal style this year by saving outfits I like and genuinely studying the similarities between them all. These zip-up boots were a common theme that kept coming up, and I knew having them would allow me to wear what I already own in new ways, so I finally snagged a pair. The break-in period is a little uncomfy, but they reminded me how much a new pair of statement shoes can make your whole wardrobe feel new again. Maybe Docs don't fit your personal style, but you can insert your choice of statement shoe here. — Katie McPherson

This ear cuff is SO pretty! It’s crystal-encrusted and sparkly, and it just instantly elevates any outfit. I really appreciate the fact that it doesn’t require a new piercing, too. I’ll admit I was worried it would either slide right off or pinch like a chip clip, but the hinged design stays put and is comfortable enough to forget you’re even wearing it. It comes in a few other fun colorways, and I’ve already got my eye on a few so I can create a sparkly little stack. — Julie Sprankles

What do you need to go with your one good outfit? How about your one perfect winter coat? This coat makes me feel so special and put together. At the same time, it is thick and long, making it warm enough and with enough coverage to get me through even the coldest days of the Montana winters where I live. I picked the navy color, and it goes with just about everything. It looks casual with jeans and fancy with a dress. — Sarah Aswell
